Introduction C-reactive protein (CRP) is an acute-phase reactant that can increase 1000-fold in systemic infections, trauma, and malignancies. CRP is mainly synthesized in the liver and is a vital component of the innate immune system. CRP is important in host defense and the clearance of apoptotic cells by binding to foreign pathogens and damaged cells. In 1930, CRP was first described by Tillet and Francis and found to be elevated in patients with pneumococcal pneumonia . The use of CRP as a diagnostic tool and marker of disease progression and treatment response has been increasingly recognized in recent years. This narrative review aimed to summarize the current state of knowledge regarding the implications of CRP in disease progression, diagnosis, and management. A comprehensive literature search was conducted using various databases including PubMed, Google Scholar, Lens, and Dimensions. The search was conducted using the following keywords: "C-reactive protein," “CRP” with "inflammation," "disease progression," "diagnosis," and "management." CRP mainly belongs to the pentraxin family of calcium-dependent ligand-binding plasma proteins, mainly found as pentamers in circulation, also known as native CRP (nCRP) . The pentameric form is primarily synthesized in hepatocytes but can also be synthesized in smooth muscle cells, macrophages, lymphocytes, and adipocytes . It also exists in its monomeric form (mCRP) in plasma , . In contrast to the pentameric form, which exerts both pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory actions, the monomeric form exerts a pro-inflammatory response in endothelial cells, endothelial progenitor cells, leukocytes, and platelets, and may amplify the inflammatory response ( ). Its synthesis is mainly induced by interleukin (IL)-6 , IL-1β, and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) . CRP binds to polysaccharides of many bacteria in the presence of calcium, which results in activation of the classic complement pathway and can promote phagocytosis and opsonization ( ). C-reactive protein (CRP) is an important component of the innate immune response. Its value deviates from the baseline by 25% and can increase 1000-fold following systemic infections, trauma, and malignancies ( ). The average CRP level in Caucasians is 0.8 mg/l, however, many factors can change the baseline levels of CRP, including age, smoking status, and weight gene polymorphism, and a study found that–35-40% change can be hereditary . 2. CRP in Disease Progression 2.1. CRP in cardiovascular disorders Many studies have discussed the importance of CRP levels in predicting the risk of cardiovascular disorders (CVD). Variation in plasma CRP levels, as an acute-phase protein, may show a retrospective view of an ischemic condition, trauma, or immune-mediated inflammation in the body, as CRP levels have been shown to deviate by approximately 25% from the original level after the onset of an inflammatory disorder ( ). This has been employed to predict the trajectories and prognostic values of several cardiovascular diseases to provide adequate management and palliative care ( ). However, when discussing CRP in the context of CVD progression, its classification as a mere downstream inflammatory marker due to the expression of IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-α has made it the focus of much scrutiny. Recently, a Mendelian randomization study conducted to clarify the role of CRP in predisposition to atherosclerosis was unable to find a direct correlation between genetic variants of CRP and coronary heart disease (CHD) risk. This relationship has been described as a reverse causation. This showed that genetically high CRP levels did not contribute as a CHD risk factor; rather, they acted as a secondary covariate associated with inflammatory responses to the disease . Inconsistent trends between ethnic differences in CRP levels and the prevalence of major cardiovascular events have prompted clinicians to question their relevance. Lastly, the ability of CRP to prognosticate recurrent MI episodes has recently been undercut by its high-half-life alternative, hs-CRP . 2.2 CRP and Autoimmunity The association of CRP with autoimmunity is highlighted when discussing the interaction of the protein with complement regulatory protein H to decrease the formation of membrane attack complexes . This diminishes the chemo-attractant ability of C5a and contributes to the minimization of tissue damage at sites of inflammation. The contributory role of CRP in the development of autoimmunity is widely debated owing to reports of diminished numbers of pathogenic autoantibodies seen in those with prolonged low-dose exposure to CRP ; however, this remains speculative. The most concrete evidence corroborating the above hypothesis is the role of CRP in the development of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) ( ). The contributory role of CRP in the development of autoimmunity is widely debated owing to reports of diminished numbers of pathogenic autoantibodies seen in those with prolonged low-dose exposure to CRP ; however, this remains speculative. The most concrete evidence corroborating the above hypothesis is the role of CRP in the development of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) ( ). In juxtaposition, CRP levels manifest differently in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA, a chronic inflammatory condition mainly affecting the joints which is variably autoimmune in origin, has employed CRP as a marker of disease activity based on the core components of the 28-joint Disease Activity Score (DAS28). The involvement of CRP in RA progression is summarized in . 2.3. CRP in infection and sepsis The manifestation of CRP levels in ongoing infectious processes, although is diagnostically important to differentiate between bacterial and viral infections, its role in determining the course of infection is also being extensively researched. CRP levels are used for risk stratification for COVID-19, Dengue Virus (DENV), and Human Immuno-deficiency Virus (HIV) infections ( ). Additionally, when discussing sepsis, the number of potential biomarkers is expansive owing to the intricacy of reactions perpetuating the event, but CRP is relatively widely used for assessing the risk of mortality, more specifically ICU mortality and organ failure . According to Lobo et al., patients with CRP levels >10 mg/dl exhibited a significant increase in renal, respiratory, and coagulation failures, along with a definitively poorer prognosis in patients with sepsis than in those with CRP levels <1 mg/dL . Serum analysis of CRP is coupled with leukocyte counts and albumin levels to obtain more accurate results. 2.4. CRP and cancer Despite the lack of substantial evidence to support this, CRP has been linked to the question of cancer causation for many years. This is due to markedly elevated levels of CRP in the disease, known to cause increased cancer cell proliferation , and the ability of the marker to accurately predict the risk of eventual cancer in previously healthy individuals ( ). The literature has shown a significant association between increased serum CRP and the presence of breast, colorectal, ovarian, prostate, and lung cancers . Other researchers have discussed the poor prognosis of melanoma, metastatic pancreatic cancer, and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma with increased CRP . More recently, an increased risk of ovarian cancer was found with CRP > 10 mg/dl within 7 years of the assay , and a high baseline CRP level (> 3 mg/L) implicated an 80% greater risk of early death from cancer . CRP analysis in the context of colorectal cancer (CRC) has shown worse overall and cancer-free survival, with a low leukocyte-to-CRP ratio (LCR) and low CRP-albumin ratio, suggesting a definitive predictive relevance for stage II/III CRC and labeling LCR as the most sensitive biomarker for cancer progression . Moreover, post-procedural CRP evaluation has shown promise in accurately predicting the peritoneal recurrence of CRC . 3. <bold>CRP in Diagnosis</bold> As an acute-phase protein, inflammation-induced CRP release is the response of the body to tissue damage and injury, which refines the role of CRP as a measure of tissue damage decontextualized in the form of inflammation. The inability of the CRP response to differentiate between the cause and effect of the pathology and the gap in the understanding of its true function has left the significance of CRP as a diagnostic marker, largely to interpretation. However, the data suggest some unification in the results that has allowed its use despite ambiguity. Most data seemed to show the increase in CRP levels post pathology to be significant within hours to days from the onset of the insult varying from 10-100 folds within 6-72 hours of the initial damage, which is the foundation of its diagnostic relevance ( ). 3.1. CRP in Infections and Sepsis Although CRP lacks diagnostic specificity, it has been widely employed to differentiate between bacterial and viral infections and to classify bacterial infections based on severity. Viral infections were associated with a lower increase in CRP levels than bacterial infections. Several studies have classified this diagnostic strategy as ‘CRP velocity’ and how it positively correlated with bacterial febrile diseases Higher CRP concentrations are also seen in lower respiratory tract infections than viral infections. This may be demonstrated by the prevalence of CRP use in confirmatory tests for community-acquired pneumonia, with a reported cutoff value of > 20 mg/L showing the greatest accuracy . In one study, CRP values > 25 mg/dL within a six-biomarker combination were able to diagnose severe bacterial infections in children with the highest sensitivity . This may be demonstrated by the prevalence of CRP use in confirmatory tests for community-acquired pneumonia, with a reported cutoff value of > 20 mg/L showing the greatest accuracy . In one study, CRP values > 25 mg/dL within a six-biomarker combination were able to diagnose severe bacterial infections in children with the highest sensitivity . CRP has also been used as a diagnostic marker of acute appendicitis .The use of CRP in diagnosing acute neonatal sepsis has shown results with a sensitivity of 76.92% , whereas in adults, CRP was able to diagnose and differentiate between sepsis with and without bacteremia, especially when used in conjunction with procalcitonin . Many developments in the rapid immunoassay of CRP for the diagnosis of neonatal sepsis are underway, which can only emphasize the diagnostic precision that it allows when discussing sepsis. Array-based electrochemical magneto-immunosensors have demonstrated promising results . Despite this, the place of the CRP assay in emergencies is currently under debate . 3.2. CRP in Osteomyelitis Osteomyelitis is one of the most prevalent complications of diabetes. Its specific and extreme implications and treatment options make accurate and timely diagnosis imperative. CRP level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) were used collectively for this purpose. While ESR serves as a more sensitive option, CRP has been reported to have the ability to differentiate between osteomyelitis and soft tissue infection, with a cutoff value of >7.9 mg/dL . A recent meta-analysis highlighted CRP as 68.5% sensitive and 70.6% specific for diagnosing diabetic foot osteomyelitis . 3.3. CRP in Inflammatory Bowel Disease Evidence has brought CRP to the spotlight when discussing the diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), providing an appropriate workup of activity in the acute phase . The positive correlation between CRP and microorganisms in the blood providing the pro-inflammatory stimulus and the strong association of CRP albumin ratio with disease progression conclusively point to its utility in IBD diagnosis and monitoring of treatment . CRP has been reported to have 78.9% sensitivity and 85.7% specificity when measured in the context of IBD, but the marker still exhibits poor clinical use owing to the unreliability of the circumstances inducing its release . 4. CRP in disease management The risk of atherosclerosis superimposed with thrombotic events is caused by two principal factors: hyperlipidaemia and inflammation. However, in a recent study published in collaboration with international randomized trials (PROMINENT, REDUCE-IT, and STRENGTH) in association with the American College of Cardiology, it was concluded that hs-CRP (high sensitivity-CRP) levels, which measure inflammation, have a greater predictive effect on atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and mortality than LDL-cholesterol levels in patients already receiving cholesterol-lowering statins . While lipid-lowering drugs to combat hypercholesterolemia are indispensable in treating and reducing cardiovascular disease risk, evidence from trials suggests that the fundamental role of the inflammatory marker CRP should be acknowledged and employed to assess cardiovascular risk, in addition to the residual risk in patients with CVD ( ). The primary future implication is that clinicians should consider both therapeutic strategies of lowering blood cholesterol levels and decreasing inflammation as having a mutually beneficial relationship in improving patient health, rather than the two strategies being used independently for treatment. For a comprehensive global evaluation of the risk of heart disease and its related comorbidities, measuring CRP level is a reliable method employed by clinicians. Individuals were grouped into low-, moderate-, and high-risk categories based on CRP values of less than 1, 1-3, and greater than 3 mg/L, respectively . CRP is used as an individual marker for atherogenesis, myocardial infarction, stroke, and cardiac arrest due to coronary heart and peripheral arterial diseases. High-sensitivity CRP is used to assess cardiovascular risk, as older tests are more suitable for detecting advanced pathological inflammatory states and are less sensitive to risk discernment. A CRP test along with a lipid panel for cholesterol measurement is necessary for patients belonging to the high CRP/low LDL category with a higher probability of developing CVD than for individuals falling in the low CRP/high LDL bracket, who would have been overlooked based on a cholesterol test alone . A CARDIA study conducted on 4405 individuals between the ages of 18-30 years proposed that management and reduction of CRP levels were positively correlated with favorable cardiac and circulatory health during the progression from adolescence to adulthood . A study showed that the best treatment for Crohn’s would be accomplished by using both CRP and Fecal Calprotectin (FCP) together . A CARDIA study conducted on 4405 individuals between the ages of 18-30 years proposed that management and reduction of CRP levels were positively correlated with favorable cardiac and circulatory health during the progression from adolescence to adulthood . A study showed that the best treatment for Crohn’s would be accomplished by using both CRP and Fecal Calprotectin (FCP) together . The importance of assessing diseases such as Crohn’s disease using inflammatory markers such as CRP is highlighted by the fact that infiltrative techniques that are prone to imprecision are more commonly employed in clinical practice. The usual practice to measure the extent of infection in inflammatory bowel disease is to perform a colonoscopy that requires extensive preparation, instrumentation, and risks of perforation as well as allergic reactions, among many others. Although colonoscopy is the mainstay for the diagnosis of Crohn’s disease, CRP as a biomarker for Crohn’s along with Fecal Calprotectin (FCP) has been shown to reduce the need for colonoscopy and its associated complications. However, increased levels of both biomarkers in the setting of reduced symptoms of disease requires confirmation with endoscopy, as does monitoring for increased severity and dysplastic changes in the epithelium ​​. This emphasizes the importance of relying on biological markers for disease management before resorting to instrumentation. A salient contribution of CRP in tracking symptom improvement in patients with Crohn’s disease receiving infliximab was observed in a previous study. A positive correlation was found between high baseline CRP levels greater than 15 mg/dl and continuance of symptoms without improvement, highlighting the ineffectiveness of infliximab therapy and prolongation of disease symptoms with higher CRP levels before treatment . Serious complications of colorectal surgery can be avoided if CRP levels are monitored during surgery, as the incidence of anastomotic leakage is correlated with increased CRP levels . The C-reactive protein to albumin ratio (CAR) has also been useful in estimating the probability of post-liver transplant complications and death . Periodic and regular CRP level measurement is a potent and advantageous technique for gauging the success of therapeutic strategies for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). CRP surpasses Fecal Calprotectin (FCP) in its dominance over the recognition and management of functional gastrointestinal disorders (FGIDs), such as IBS . A range of studies suggest that decreased CRP levels are indicative of the course of improvement of a disease condition, prediction of recovery, better future health, and an ameliorated patient response to treatment . According to a study that monitored patients with IBD, CRP levels were more specific for Crohn’s than for ulcerative colitis. CRP levels also predict the likelihood of surgery in patients with both ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease . Modulation of CRP levels and vigilant assessment can also prevent autoimmune disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, where elevated CRP levels are suggestive of aggravation of symptoms. CRP is an essential element of many RA-related scales, indices, and criteria that provides a comprehensive understanding of disease progression and treatment . A systematic review of biomarkers associated with RA concluded that a substandard response to conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) for RA was indicated with CRP levels >7.1 mg/L . CRP, rheumatoid factor (RF), and anti-CRP antibodies help investigate treatment strategies for rheumatoid arthritis indicated by the following diagram ( ). Studies attributing depression to pervasive inflammation have implied that high concentrations of highly sensitive hs-CRP may be detected in blood and cerebrospinal fluid . In a study to detect the presence of secondary infection in COVID-19 patients using CRP and PCT, it was suggested that a rise or fall in CRP levels can predict the presence or absence of hospital-acquired infection in patients with COVID-19 and may necessitate antibiotic therapy . CRP point-of-care testing is recognized as an important test used in outpatient departments to reduce reliance on antibiotics . Patients with a lower respiratory tract infection and prominent symptoms of fever with high CRP levels were directed towards antibiotics in a CRP Point-of Care Testing (POCT) . The C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR) was recognized in a recent study as a marker of respiratory failure in Guillain Barre syndrome, with CAR>0.21 having a positive correlation and CAR>0.19, coinciding with an increased risk of aggressive disease with a low prospect of recuperation . If effectively controlled, the CAR ratio can also prevent respiratory complications in P. falciparum malaria. Increased CRP to Albumin Ratio in adults has implicated worse prognosis and respiratory complications due to imported falciparum malaria . A systematic review and meta-analysis compared CRP, procalcitonin (PCT), IL-8, and TNF-α in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with the following results ( ). Increased CRP to Albumin Ratio in adults has implicated worse prognosis and respiratory complications due to imported falciparum malaria . A systematic review and meta-analysis compared CRP, procalcitonin (PCT), IL-8, and TNF-α in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with the following results ( ). A study that measured CRP levels in the saliva and serum of children with acute respiratory illness suggested a positive correlation between salivary and serum CRP levels, suggesting that salivary CRP accurately indicates high serum CRP levels, thereby virtually minimizing the need for phlebotomy in children . As rising CRP levels have been positively implicated in a plethora of inflammatory diseases, a sensible assumption would be to reduce these levels to restrict the progression of these diseases and possibly help provide more proficient treatment. Various studies have shown that reducing the hepatic synthesis of CRP by directly inhibiting CRP mRNA translation successfully lowered CRP levels using Anti Streptolysin-O titers (ASO) in humans and experimental rats . Another approach utilizing 1,6-bis(phosphocholine)-hexane reduced the size of infarcts and exhibited a cardioprotective role by suppressing the exacerbation of the negative effects in experimental mice in which myocardial infarction was stimulated. This was achieved by preventing the binding of CRP to its ligands, enhancing its excretion, and reducing complement-mediated inflammatory effects . However, CRP also exhibits the potential to aggregate with 1,6-bis (phosphocholine)-hexane molecules and accumulate in the vessels, causing detrimental effects and possibly activating further inflammatory side effects. Immunosuppression is a more threatening clinical consideration when targeting CRP for disease management using this compound. CRP apheresis is an effective extracorporeal therapeutic advancement that can be employed to directly direct its effects on CRP without interfering with the levels of other markers of inflammation . This technique proved successful in lowering CRP levels in patients with myocardial infarction but showed nonspecific results in patients with COVID-19 . To test whether CRP lowering can have beneficial effects in the management of acute kidney injury and in patients receiving kidney transplants, a study using CRP transgenic mice compared to wild-type mice explored the effects of inducing ischemia-reperfusion injury in these mice. The results indicated that targeting CRP for kidney injury can be a valuable intervention, since it was shown to exacerbate tubular damage and promote its transition from acute to chronic kidney disease . Transgenic mice before ischemia-reperfusion injury did not show grossly elevated CRP levels and thus did not display significant clinical manifestations of Acute Kidney Injury either . The link between inflammation and malignancy has been corroborated and reinforced by various studies. Elevated CRP levels are strong indicators of poor prognosis in cancer treatment. A study on patients with oesophageal cancer emphasized the prognostic value of serum CRP in assessing patient response and survival . A study observing the quality of life of patients post-treatment for endometrial cancer suggested that CRP measurement, along with other markers such as GPS and CAR pre- and postoperatively, has a notable prognostic significance in judging disease-related mortality, recurrence, management, and response to treatment . Shinohara et al.’s study on lung cancer also showed improved patient survival in the group of patients with CRP levels <5 mg/L after surgery . Hence, CRP assessment has helped in increasing success in cancer survival and mitigation of worsening exacerbation or recrudescence of the disease. 5. Limitations and future discussion The indisputable potential of CRP as a marker for diagnosis, disease progression, prognostic indicators, and follow-up of outcomes to treatment regimens has been authenticated by numerous studies on the pathogenic mechanisms and prevention of various diseases. The novel role of CRP in appraising the success of medical interventions for treating IBD has been demonstrated; however, it is less reliable in patients with milder diseases who may not have significant elevations in the diagnosis of mucosal healing .Leucine-rich alpha-2 glycoprotein is regarded as a more important biomarker than CRP for tissue damage and inflammation in Crohn’s disease . Multiple studies have reported that CRP level alone is not sufficient to predict morbidity or mortality in disease states, and CAR provides a more accurate prediction . Nonetheless, the specificity of CAR is compromised because CRP and albumin levels are independently affected by different factors. A study has also proposed that the invasive method of assessing CRP levels for cardiovascular disease from a blood sample can be replaced with the Bi-Digital O-Ring Test Resonance Phenomenon using L-homocysteine, especially for circumstances in which CRP levels are not indicative of any underlying pathology . High CRP levels are found in certain neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and age-related macular degeneration . A study has also proposed that the invasive method of assessing CRP levels for cardiovascular disease from a blood sample can be replaced with the Bi-Digital O-Ring Test Resonance Phenomenon using L-homocysteine, especially for circumstances in which CRP levels are not indicative of any underlying pathology . High CRP levels are found in certain neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and age-related macular degeneration . A comprehensive understanding of how CRP levels are associated with the development and progression of these diseases is not completely understood or ascertained in comparison with its clear association with more prevalent disorders, as discussed above. Further exploration is imperative to establish the importance of CRP as a prognosticator for effective management of these diseases. The role of CRP in the diagnosis of complicated disease processes and investigating effective treatment modalities for them cannot be negated; nevertheless, it is imperative to mention that it is a non-specific marker of inflammation, which may either be the causative factor underlying the pathogenesis of a disease, simply associated with it, or come forth as one of its associated complications. Hence, sole reliance on the measurement of this inflammatory marker to understand disease causes, progression, and treatment response is often neglected as more specific markers for diseases have been identified and compared in their effectiveness with CRP. Having established that the most effective clinical investigations regarding diseases employ multiple testing parameters assessing CRP along with disease-specific markers to comprehensively probe the complexities that underlie the diseases, and that relying on either disease marker alone would not yield. 6. Conclusion CRP In conclusion, this review aimed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the C-reactive protein (CRP) role as a biomarker for disease progression, diagnosis, and management. Studies have indicated that changes in CRP levels can reflect the severity of inflammation and predict the risk of developing chronic inflammatory disease. The significance of CRP as a diagnostic tool is enhanced by understanding its association with the development of diabetes, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and autoimmune diseases. CRP levels are predictive of future outcomes in various populations including healthy individuals and high-risk patients. Despite the constraints in interpreting the CRP results, including the necessity for multiple tests and potential interfering variables, its practical value cannot be disregarded. In general, understanding the effects of CRP levels on disease progression, diagnosis, and management can result in enhanced patient care and outcomes. documents.title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Treatment

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC In the past year, diverse associations published new recommendations for the initial management of lupus nephritis (LN) that include four first-line immunosuppressive regimens. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS Through a scoping review, we explore the evidence gaps from randomised controlled trials in LN, the heterogeneity in study designs and under-represented groups in current knowledge. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY This study provides the rationale for evaluating unexplored treatment comparisons and conducting studies on newer interventions in clinical settings where evidence is lacking. Introduction In the past year, significant updates were made to the guidelines for the management of lupus nephritis (LN). Key organisations, such as the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR), the Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) group and the Spanish Group for the Study of Glomerular Diseases (GLOSEN), now recommend a combination of glucocorticoids with one of four options of immunosuppressive regimens for initial LN therapy. The updated recommendations introduce triple immunosuppressive regimens, which consist of glucocorticoids plus one of the following combinations: calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) such as voclosporin or tacrolimus plus mycophenolic acid analogues (MPAAs); or belimumab with either cyclophosphamide (CYC) or MPAA. These triple schemes emerge as an attractive alternative to the traditional double immunosuppressive regimens consisting of glucocorticoids in combination with CYC (oral or intravenous following the Euro-Lupus Nephritis Trial (ELNT) or modified National Institute of Health (NIH) protocols) or MPAA. However, except for some suggestions mentioned in these documents, the choice of which treatment regimen to use is left to the clinician’s judgement ( ). Of note, the terms ‘double’ and ‘triple regimens’ do not encompass all treatments typically prescribed to patients with LN, since antimalarials and/or other non-immune therapies (eg, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors) are generally recommended as adjuncts to any treatment scheme, unless contraindicated. The evidence behind current guidelines is derived from randomised clinical trials (RCTs) that evaluated these interventions across highly variable settings. Many of these trials involved distinct populations with specific selection criteria that make it difficult to extrapolate their results to the general population. External validity is the extent to which results from a study can be generalised to other settings, clinical presentations and populations that were not included in the original study. It is plausible that some trials may have limited external validity, thereby reducing the applicability of clinical guideline recommendations to certain patient groups. Additionally, not all treatment regimens, especially the newer triple schemes, have been compared head-to-head or evaluated in all real-world settings, making it challenging for clinicians to select the most appropriate treatment for different clinical scenarios. Here, we performed a scoping review of RCTs assessing initial pharmacological LN therapies, focusing on the study design, selected populations and outcome definitions, to assess the generalisability of their results and describe gaps in the evidence. Methods We aimed to assemble and characterise the existing RCTs evaluating initial treatment of LN. This scoping review follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) recommendations. Patient and the public were not involved in the conduct of this study. Eligibility criteria were primary RCTs evaluating pharmacological interventions for the initial treatment of LN that included adult subjects and were published between January 2000 and February 2024. This period includes clinical trials using current standard of care (SoC) regimens as comparator in most clinical trials. RCTs with combined adult and paediatric populations were eligible for inclusion. We excluded non-randomised studies, studies evaluating LN as a secondary endpoint (eg, SLE trials also studying LN, kidney disease trials that included participants with LN), trials exclusively evaluating maintenance treatment, secondary publications of RCTs with a previously published primary outcome, studies with less than 10 participants, studies with entirely paediatric population and studies published in a language different from English, Spanish or French. We opted to exclude small studies since they were more likely to represent prematurely terminated RCTs or RCTs without results and because most sample size calculations for testing two therapies typically exceed 10–20 subjects. In addition, understanding the implications of limiting our search by language, the decision was made due to the feasibility of conducting the review. We searched MEDLINE (PubMed), CENTRAL, Scopus and Web of Science on 15 February 2024. The complete search strategy is found in the supplemental material. To corroborate that our search strategy yielded, at minimum, the most clinically relevant records, we performed citation searching in the latest updated KDIGO Lupus Nephritis Guidelines. No new records were added. Two independent researchers (AN-G and GC-K) performed data charting in two phases: first, title and abstract screening of the retrieved records; second, full-text review to assess eligibility. Disagreements were settled by dialogue between researchers or by a third independent reviewer (JMM-V). We employed Rayyan Software ( http://rayyan.qcri.org/ ) for data charting. We extracted

To corroborate that our search strategy yielded, at minimum, the most clinically relevant records, we performed citation searching in the latest updated KDIGO Lupus Nephritis Guidelines. No new records were added. Two independent researchers (AN-G and GC-K) performed data charting in two phases: first, title and abstract screening of the retrieved records; second, full-text review to assess eligibility. Disagreements were settled by dialogue between researchers or by a third independent reviewer (JMM-V). We employed Rayyan Software ( http://rayyan.qcri.org/ ) for data charting. We extracted the following variables from the included RCTs into a spreadsheet: authors, publication year, journal, journal impact factor (jcr.clarivate.com), recruitment years, study design characteristics (allocation, blinding, follow-up time, inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria, primary outcome definitions, secondary outcomes), interventions, characteristics of each intervention arm (drug, participants allocated to each group, participants receiving the intervention), sociodemographic characteristics (age, sex, race, ethnicity, geographical region), participant clinical characteristics (time from diagnosis, previous renal flares, kidney function markers, disease severity, SLE activity markers), and histological characteristics of the kidney biopsy (activity and chronicity indices, histological classification (ISN/RPS)). We reviewed trial registries for missing data (clinicaltrials.gov or clinicaltrialsregister.eu). We evaluated each RCT arm separately; thus, a single RCT could contribute two or more intervention arms to the study. We categorised each arm based on whether they evaluated guideline-recommended regimens (CYC (NIH, ELNT or oral), MPAA, CNI plus MPAA, or belimumab plus MPAA/CYC) or other initial therapy regimens (such as azathioprine, leflunomide, rituximab, obinutuzumab, ocrelizumab, among others). We used frequencies and percentages to describe evidence gaps and representation of different groups. We used SPSS V.24.0 (IBM, New York, USA) and GraphPad Prism V.9.5.0 (GraphPad Software, California, USA) for analyses. Since the primary objective of the present study was to identify potential gaps in evidence and representation in LN RCTs, we critically appraised individual sources of evidence. For this purpose, we reviewed outcome definitions, inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria and reporting of participant clinical characteristics. In addition, we calculated the Fragility Index (FI) to analyse the robustness of statistically significant RCT results, the Reverse Fragility Index (RFI) to analyse statistically non-significant results using the method described by Khan et al , and the fragility quotient (FQ) by dividing the FI or the RFI by the sample size. Briefly, the FI represents the minimum number of participants whose status would need to change from an event to a non-event for the study to lose statistical significance; while the RFI represents the opposite, the number of participants whose status would need to change from a non-event to an event for the study to gain statistical significance. We used the R Project ‘Fragility’ package to calculate these indices. Further specification of this analysis is provided in the . Results The search strategy yielded 2010 results, of which 675 were duplicate records. Of the remaining 1335 trials, 1274 were excluded in the abstract screening and full-text review phases, resulting in 61 included RCTs ( and ). Selected trials were published from 2000 to 2024, with recruitment periods from 1992 to 2020. The included RCTs had a population of 7058 participants, with the smallest including 15 subjects and the largest 446. Among the 61 trials, 124 intervention arms were analysed (59 experimental and 65 control groups). In the studies comparing different doses of prednisone within the same treatment regimen, all groups were considered as controls. Within the 124 intervention arms studied, 79 (63.7%) evaluated guideline-recommended initial treatment regimens in 4522 participants (64.1%). MPAA was the most commonly studied intervention, administered to 1885 participants (26.7%) in 33 intervention arms, followed closely by the modified NIH CYC regimen, which was evaluated in 1289 participants (18.3%) in 28 study arms. Triple immunosuppressive regimens using CNIs or belimumab were studied in 925 participants (13.1%) in seven intervention arms. The remaining 2536 participants (35.9%) received other initial treatment schemes not currently considered as SoC, including B-cell depleting therapies, other CNI-based schemes, non-guideline-recommended CYC regimens and other biologic therapies ( ). Study design and selection criteria Most RCTs were multicentre (n=36, 59.0%), of which 19 (31.1%) were multinational. Follow-up of 12 months or longer was observed in 29 trials (47.5%), and only 9 RCTs (14.8%) followed patients for 24 months or longer ( ). The geographical distribution of study interventions varied significantly. Some treatments, such as MPAA, NIH, and ELNT CYC regimens, were evaluated in trials that included participants from all World Bank geographical regions. Others, like voclosporin and belimumab, included centres from most regions. Meanwhile, interventions like tacrolimus and oral CYC were predominantly, or exclusively in the case of tacrolimus, tested in centres in Asia. Fifty-eight (95.1%) studies required a kidney biopsy showing active disease for inclusion. Thirty (49.2%) studies considered proteinuria ≥1 g/day as inclusion criteria, 13 (21.3%) ≥1.5 g/day, and only five trials (8.2%) included only participants with a baseline proteinuria ≥2 g/day. Baseline proteinuria was determined by 24-hour urine collection in most studies, with only nine RCTs (28.1%) using spot urine protein-creatinine ratio (uPCR) to estimate daily proteinuria. Ten (16.4%) studies were performed exclusively in severe or refractory disease (as defined by the investigators), and five (8.2%) were restricted to newly diagnosed LN. Only the NIH-based and MPAA-based regimens have been evaluated in clinical trials limited to a population with severe or treatment-refractory presentations, as defined by the investigators. Furthermore, these are the only two regimens studied in RCTs that exclusively included participants with baseline proteinuria ≥2 g/day. Twenty (32.8%), 16 (26.2%) and 3 (4.9%) RCTs established their eGFR exclusion criteria cut-offs at ≤20, ≤30 or ≤45 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , respectively. Few studies included the chronicity index, ≥50% glomeruli with sclerosis, or crescents as an exclusion criterion. Voclosporin has only been studied in participants with a baseline eGFR >45 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , and belimumab in participants with >30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Half of all trials evaluating triple therapy with tacrolimus excluded participants with chronicity index ≥4, and 25% excluded those with ≥3 points. Fifty-five (90.2%) studies evaluated efficacy by either complete response (CR) or overall response (OR) to treatment. Only nine trials evaluated histological response to treatment through repeat kidney biopsies, three of which were secondary, or subgroup analyses not included among the original 61 RCTs. Safety outcomes were variably reported, with only 29 (47.5%) studies reporting serious adverse events, and 27 (44.3%) severe infections. Secondary outcomes such as progression to kidney failure and kidney flares were evaluated in 8 (13.1%) and 17 (27.9%) studies, respectively. None of the studies included patient-reported outcomes (PRO) in their primary efficacy definition. Although PROs were potentially evaluated in several RCTs, these were detailed in only 8 of 61 (13.1%) RCTs. Population characteristics Sex, race and ethnicity, geographical region and histopathological classification of LN information was available for 96.6%, 81.0%, 89.1% and 92.1% of participants, respectively. Overall, 86.5% of all RCT participants were female. Asians were the most represented race in the clinical trials, comprising 55.2% of the participants, followed by White, representing 28.4% of participants. Black and other races composed only 7.2% and 9.2% of participants in RCTs, respectively. All interventions included participants of all races, except for tacrolimus plus MPAA, where 100% of participants evaluated in RCTs were classified as Asian. Hispanic/Latino ethnicity was reported in 13.7% of participants, none of them included in RCTs that evaluated oral CYC or triple therapy with tacrolimus. The geographical region that comprised the most participants of RCTs was Southeast Asia and Pacific (n=3715, 59.1%), followed by North America (n=800, 12.7%), Europe and Central Asia (n=790, 12.5%), and Latin America and the Caribbean (n=729, 12.0%). Few participants were from the Middle East and North Africa (n=236, 3.9%) and sub-Saharan Africa (n=18, 0.3%). No participants from sub-Saharan Africa were included in any of the clinical trials of guideline-recommended therapies. Middle East and North African populations were represented only in trials evaluating MPAA, NIH and ELNT CYC regimens, and in a low proportion. RCTs mainly comprised participants with International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society (ISN/RPS) ‘proliferative’ classes of LN (classes III/IV±V). Only 615 (9.5%) participants had pure class V LN. All RCTs that evaluated guideline-recommended schemes, except for oral CYC, included ISN/RPS class V LN participants. Out of the 36 multicentre trials, only in 5 (13.9%) studied the renal biopsy specimens were blindly re-evaluated by a central study pathologist. Definitions of study outcomes There was high variability in the definitions of efficacy outcomes used by LN clinical trials. All studies defined a threshold of proteinuria necessary to consider CR to treatment, and 93.4% of the trials also required improvement, return to baseline or normalisation of kidney function. However, some studies had additional requirements, such as an inactive urinary sediment, normalisation of serum albumin or adherence to certain immunosuppression regulations (ie, no use of rescue therapies, adherence to prednisone taper, etc). Older studies tended to use lower proteinuria thresholds. Specifically, 19 (61.3%) treatment arms of trials published before 2012 used 0.4 g/24 hours or lower as the cut-off point for proteinuria, whereas 25 (31.2%) intervention arms of studies published after 2012 applied this same threshold (see ). Eight (24.2%) study arms receiving MPAA-based regimens, eight (28.6%) receiving NIH CYC regimen and two (66.7%) allocated to oral CYC were evaluated using a stricter definition of CR requiring a decrease in proteinuria below 0.3 g/24 hours, in contrast to none in the other guideline-recommended regimens. The most frequent definition of CR required the return of kidney function within 30% of its baseline and proteinuria ≤0.5 g/24 hours, which was applied to 3299 (48.2%) participants comprising all guideline-recommended regimens. Most participants (n=209, 60.4%) allocated to triple therapy with tacrolimus were evaluated using a CR definition that required proteinuria below 0.4 g/24 hours and normal renal function. Similarly, the most used definition of partial response (PR), applied to 44.4% of participants, required a return of renal function within 30% of its baseline and a ≥50% reduction in proteinuria to <3.0 g/24 hours. Further characterisation of efficacy outcomes definitions is available in . Reporting of baseline characteristics The reporting of baseline characteristics that could impact efficacy outcomes varied significantly among LN RCTs ( ). Only 23 (37.7%) and 15 (24.6%) RCTs reported the mean time since diagnosis and number of participants that had previous kidney flares, respectively. Fifty-one trials (83.6%) reported mean baseline proteinuria and eGFR or serum creatinine (SCr) of participants in each intervention group. However, reporting of the number of participants within each eGFR and proteinuria range (eg, number of participants with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , or proteinuria in the nephrotic range) was poor. Almost all trials (n=58, 95.1%) described the ISN/RPS histopathological class of LN of the participants in each group, but few reported the baseline chronicity indices, or other prognostically relevant histopathological variables, such as number of patients with crescents or sclerosis in >50% of glomeruli. Concomitant use of other drugs that affect proteinuria was reported in only 17 (27.9%) RCTs for angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) and in 4 (6.6%) trials for antimalarials. Head-to-head comparisons of guideline-recommended initial therapy regimens shows a heatmap based on the number of trials that performed direct comparisons between guideline-recommended schemes. Notably, while MPAA has been compared with all guideline-recommended schemes except for tacrolimus plus MPAA; some therapies (oral CYC, tacrolimus plus MPAA, voclosporin plus MPAA) have exclusively been directly compared with only one other scheme. There are no studies comparing triple immunosuppressive regimens against each other. Robustness of RCTs evaluating initial treatment of LN The FI and RFI were variable across studies, ranging from 1 to 20. Most non-inferiority trials between the modified NIH versus ELNT schemes, NIH versus MPAA, and ELNT versus MPAA schemes showed no significant difference in efficacy outcomes between each other. Those head-to-head RCTs between double immunosuppressive regimens that did have statistically significant results, demonstrated low FI (1 to 3). Trials comparing triple immunosuppressive therapies versus SoC showed very high FI, especially those using CNI. Liu et al , the largest trial evaluating tacrolimus, demonstrated a FI of 18 for CR at 6 months. AURORA-1, the phase III trial evaluating voclosporin, demonstrated a FI of 15 for CR at 12 months. This means that, for the results of these studies to lose statistical significance, 18 participants who received triple therapy with tacrolimus and achieved CR at 6 months, and 15 participants who received triple therapy with voclosporin and achieved CR at 12 months, would have had to fail to respond to their respective treatments. Discussion Given the broad spectrum of clinical presentations and the heterogeneity of patients affected by LN, guideline developers face the great challenge of ensuring that this diverse population is adequately represented in terms of their sociodemographic and clinical characteristics. Although the guidelines mention the primary groups in which each regimen has been studied, no in-depth analysis of the external validity of these recommendations has been performed. In this scoping review, which encompasses 61 initial LN therapy RCTs involving more than 7000 participants, we identified several under-represented groups, interventions that have not been assessed across all real-world settings, and a lack of head-to-head comparisons between most treatment regimens ( ). Box 1 Key findings and proposed suggestions Key findings: Evidence gaps and under-represented groups Participants identifying as Black, Hispanic and other races (American Indian, Pacific Islander, etc) were significantly under-represented in lupus nephritis RCTs. Participants from sub-Saharan Africa, Middle East and North Africa, and Latin America and the Caribbean were insufficiently represented. Triple therapy with tacrolimus has only been studied among Asians in single-country, open-label trials. Only CYC-NIH and MPAA regimens have been studied exclusively in patients with severe/refractory disease. Triple regimens have been evaluated entirely in patients with relatively preserved renal function and/or low chronicity indices. Less than 50% of the studies reported serious adverse events, and only 13% included patient-reported outcomes. Complete response to treatment was variably defined, with studies before 2012 mainly using a proteinuria cut-off of 0.3 g/24 hours, and after 2012 0.5 g/24 hours or higher. There is no consensus on whether other parameters should be included in the definition of CR (eGFR, inactive urinary sediment, adherence to immunosuppression regulations, etc). Most therapies (oral CYC, tacrolimus plus MPAA, voclosporin plus MPAA) have exclusively been directly compared with only one other scheme. There are no studies comparing triple immunosuppressive regimens against each other. Conclusions and proposed suggestions We call for a broader inclusion of under-represented populations as participants in LN RCTs. The study design should be homogenised, ensuring consistent description of relevant baseline characteristics, standardisation of efficacy outcomes definitions and uniform assessment of other outcomes (safety profile, PRO). Newer interventions should be assessed in clinical settings where evidence is currently lacking, and unexplored treatment comparisons should be evaluated head-to-head. CR, complete response.; CYC, cyclophosphamide; eGFR, estimated glomerular filtration rate; LN, lupus nephritis; MPAA, mycophenolic acid analogsanalogues; NIH, National Institutes of Health; PRO, patient-reported outcomes; RCT, randomizedrandomised clinicalontrolled trial. A significant under-representation of several population groups was observed. Participants identifying as Black and Hispanic comprised only 7.2% and 13.7% of all participants, respectively, despite reports indicating that these populations are at higher risk for developing earlier and more severe LN, with increased rates of kidney failure and mortality. Asian and White race accounted for ≥80% of the population in clinical trials of all guideline-recommended regimens, with some schemes like triple therapy using tacrolimus, being evaluated exclusively among Asians. Less than 5% of all participants were from the Middle East, North Africa or Sub-Saharan Africa, even though recent studies indicate that the prevalence in these regions is significantly higher than previously estimated, calculated at 1.7%. However, this number is likely underestimated due to the scarcity of epidemiological studies and specialists in these regions. These disparities raise concerns about whether the recommendations in the guidelines can truly be extended to these under-represented populations. In contrast, other sociodemographic characteristics were adequately represented. The ratio of female to male participants in the trials closely resembled the relation seen in clinical practice, as 86.5% of participants were female, approximating the ratio of 9:1 seen in SLE. Similarly, in terms of the histopathological classification of LN, the relation of membranous to proliferative cases matched the distribution seen in clinical practice. It is estimated that 10–15% of LN cases are class V, a proportion observed in the studies of most guideline-recommended regimens, except for the ELNT CYC regimen, where this group was slightly underrepresented, and oral CYC, where it was completely omitted. Not all guideline-recommended interventions have been evaluated in all real-world settings, resulting in multiple gaps in the evidence. For instance, NIH CYC regimen and triple therapy with tacrolimus have only been assessed in single-country, open-label trials. Conversely, studies evaluating triple therapy with belimumab or voclosporin, despite being limited in number, are methodologically robust, multicentre, multinational, double-blind RCTs. Another gap in the evidence is that some regimens have not been evaluated across the full spectrum of LN severity. NIH and MPAA,

except for the ELNT CYC regimen, where this group was slightly underrepresented, and oral CYC, where it was completely omitted. Not all guideline-recommended interventions have been evaluated in all real-world settings, resulting in multiple gaps in the evidence. For instance, NIH CYC regimen and triple therapy with tacrolimus have only been assessed in single-country, open-label trials. Conversely, studies evaluating triple therapy with belimumab or voclosporin, despite being limited in number, are methodologically robust, multicentre, multinational, double-blind RCTs. Another gap in the evidence is that some regimens have not been evaluated across the full spectrum of LN severity. NIH and MPAA, as the oldest recommended interventions and the most extensively studied drugs, are the only treatments that have been assessed in trials composed exclusively of patients with severe or refractory disease. Meanwhile, newer treatment schemes have only been assessed in participants with less severe LN. Specifically, voclosporin and belimumab have been evaluated entirely in patients with relatively preserved renal function, while tacrolimus has primarily been studied in participants with low chronicity indices. Lower baseline eGFR and higher chronicity indices are factors that have consistently been associated with worse renal outcomes and response to treatment, thus the importance of evaluating these newer interventions in participants with these characteristics. In addition to baseline eGFR and chronicity indices, other factors like previous kidney flares, elevated baseline proteinuria and concomitant use of ACEi/ARBs or antimalarials can also affect renal outcomes and response to treatment and are therefore important to report as baseline characteristics of trial participants. However, the reporting of these variables was generally poor, appearing in less than 50% of studies. The absence of this information hinders clinicians’ ability to interpret trial results objectively. Even more concerning, we found no correlation between the amount of these variables reported and the year of publication of the RCTs, suggesting that a trend towards increased description and transparency of baseline characteristics of participants has not yet become standard practice. Another challenge in objectively interpreting the results of LN RCTs is the wide variation in efficacy outcome definitions used by investigators. Trials evaluating older interventions, like MPAA, NIH and oral CYC, tended to use stricter thresholds of proteinuria for defining CR, whereas newer schemes like voclosporin and belimumab, settled with a 0.5 g/24 hours cut-off point or higher. This variability in the definition of CR used can significantly alter study results. Wofsy et al demonstrated that by using different definitions of CR in the same study, it is possible to obtain drastically different remission rates. The BMS trial, which used a stricter criterion requiring proteinuria below 0.26 g/g, return of eGFR within 10% of the baseline value, and normal urinary sediment, reported a CR of 4% for the combined abatacept groups, with no benefit over the control group. Meanwhile, if the investigators had used the definition employed by the ACCESS trial, which required a proteinuria below 0.5 g/g and return of eGFR within 25% of the baseline value, a CR would have been observed in 39.8% of participants, demonstrating an advantage over the SoC. Similarly, BLISS-LN, the phase III RCT evaluating triple therapy with belimumab, assessed response at 104 weeks using two different criteria. The first and laxer definition (termed primary efficacy renal response) required a proteinuria <0.7 g/g and an eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 or within 20% of the pre-flare value, which yielded a response in 43% of participants. The stricter definition (termed CR) used a proteinuria cut-off point of 0.5 g/g with an eGFR ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m 2 or within 10% of the baseline value, resulting in a 13% decrease in the observed response rate. This heterogeneity in the definitions and terms of efficacy outcomes complicates the comparison between treatment regimens and suggests that trials involving newer therapies might have reached different conclusions if alternative definitions had been used. Additionally, it is also concerning that only nine trials assessed histological response to treatment through repeat kidney biopsies. Recent studies have shown that standard clinical and laboratory parameters for evaluating treatment response do not reliably indicate cessation of histological damage in the kidneys, as up to one-third of patients with absent proteinuria, inactive urinary sediment or an abnormal eGFR may still exhibit ongoing disease activity. Therefore, until new and reliable biomarkers for disease activity are approved, repeat kidney biopsies remain an important tool for objectively evaluating treatment response. The last decades have observed growing interest in patient’s perspective of their disease by measuring PRO and their inclusion in the regulatory process for drug approval and labelling. A study from the European Medicines Agency observed that only 48.3% of authorised drugs in the period of 2017 to 2022 reported PROs, with variability among medical areas. until new and reliable biomarkers for disease activity are approved, repeat kidney biopsies remain an important tool for objectively evaluating treatment response. The last decades have observed growing interest in patient’s perspective of their disease by measuring PRO and their inclusion in the regulatory process for drug approval and labelling. A study from the European Medicines Agency observed that only 48.3% of authorised drugs in the period of 2017 to 2022 reported PROs, with variability among medical areas. SLE and LN have significant impacts on patient’s health-related quality of life. We observed that only 13.1% of RCTs included PROs in their final report which underlines an unmet need. While there are initiatives to integrate PRO into clinical outcome assessments in SLE trials, this seems challenging for LN RCTs as extrarenal symptoms may have more impact on these measurements. The FI is a valuable tool for assessing the robustness of RCT results. According to this metric, pivotal trials evaluating guideline-recommended triple therapies exhibited marked superiority over double schemes. Nonetheless, it remains to be determined whether these outcomes are sustained when replicated in populations where they have not been studied yet, such as those with exclusively severe or refractory disease, individuals with more chronic renal damage or previous kidney flares, and unexplored sociodemographic groups. Additionally, head-to-head comparisons between triple schemes need to be conducted. As was the case with MPAA and NIH CYC schemes, the aim is to promote the development of new clinical trials that directly compare these regimens and evaluate them across diverse populations and clinical settings, to identify the most appropriate treatment for each specific scenario. Our study presents several limitations. The exclusion of non-randomised clinical trials, secondary studies, RCTs evaluating paediatric populations only and studies published in other languages or databases not consulted in this review represents a considerable amount of research that could have affected the findings in this study. Nevertheless, we found only one RCT excluded by language. Another limitation is the inconsistency in the reporting of baseline characteristics and outcomes, given that geographical region was not reported in more than 10% of participants, and race and ethnicity in almost 20%. Variables that impact efficacy outcomes could only be analysed if they were reported as categorical variables (sex, race, histopathological class, selection criteria, previous kidney flares, etc). Those reported as continuous variables, including mean/median baseline proteinuria, eGFR, chronicity indices, among others, could not be included in the analysis. Additionally, the glucocorticoid regimen used in each trial was not described. The objective of this comprehensive study was to gather the pivotal clinical trials pertaining to the initial management of LN, elucidating the current body of evidence and identifying gaps that need to be addressed. This analysis now paves the way for a network meta-analysis to be conducted, which will enable a comparative evaluation of the efficacy of guideline-recommended treatment protocols. Considering new recommendations for the management of LN, we call for broader inclusion of under-represented populations and homogenisation of study designs. Our goal is for this study to serve as a rationale for evaluating unexplored treatment comparisons and conducting studies on newer interventions in clinical settings where evidence is currently lacking. supplementary material 10.1136/lupus-2024-001331 online supplemental file 1
