Gp130 expression in peripheral sensory neurons is essential for pathological pain development, including inflammatory and neuropathic pain. Activation by IL‐6 family cytokines triggers JAK/STAT signaling, upregulating pronociceptive ion channels such as TRPA1 and TRPV1 in DRG, thereby enhancing excitability and promoting mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity [ ]. Genetic deletion of gp130 in nociceptors leads to reduced hypersensitivity and downregulation of TRPA1, particularly in uninjured neurons adjacent to nerve injury, underscoring its role in driving central sensitization [ ]. The soluble gp130 (sgp130) molecule works by antagonizing IL‐6 trans‐signaling. It achieves this by binding to IL‐6/sIL‐6R complexes, effectively sequestering them and preventing their interaction with membrane‐bound gp130. Thus, it would dampen IL‐6‐mediated pronociceptive signaling as well as the upregulation of ion channels, and this could probably explain central sensitization [ ]. The fusion protein sgp130Fc, which mimics endogenous sgp130, has been proven to possess analgesic capabilities in neuropathic pain models; more specifically, it reduces glial activation as well as cytokine production and central sensitization without suppressing peripheral immunity [ ]. Intervention specificity would be an attractive characteristic to exploit in similar conditions observed both in fibromyalgia and chronic post‐inflammatory pain. Targeting gp130 also affects other IL‐6 family cytokines, including LIF and oncostatin M, which may contribute to pain modulation. However, caution is warranted to avoid disrupting the beneficial homeostatic functions of classic IL‐6 signaling [ ]. In conclusion, gp130 critically modulates ion channel expression and neuronal excitability in pain pathways. Its soluble form, sgp130, serves as a natural brake on IL‐6 trans‐signaling, offering a promising therapeutic strategy for chronic pain driven by central sensitization. 5 Clinical Evidence: <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">IL</styled-content>‐6 Inhibitors for Pain Relief Pain is the most common and one of the key symptoms in patients with RA. Up to now, most treatment strategies in RA have aimed to control inflammation and, consequently, incidentally, pain. However, pain is frequently present in this patient population despite inflammation control. Although disease activity scores in RA involve pain assessment, it appears that pain should be considered an entity independent of inflammation [ ]. Rapid onset of pain relief following IL‐6 blockade is a practical consequence that supports the thesis of non‐inflammatory anti‐IL‐6 effect [ ]. Recently, it has been shown that the JAK inhibitor baricitinib improved pain independently of inflammation in RA patients. It exerted its effect by suppressing the IL‐6 signal pathway [ , ]. It also has a role in sleep improvement, depression control, cardiovascular risk, and many other systemic, extraarticular, and metabolic processes in the body [ , , ]. Patients with high baseline IL‐6 levels, compared to those with low baseline IL‐6 levels, reported greater improvements in health‐related quality of life (HRQoL), including physical component summary (PCS), physical functioning domain, and AM‐stiffness scores, with SAR treatment compared to adalimumab [ ]. Drugs that act on the IL‐6 pathway mediate their effect as IL‐6 inhibitors or IL‐6 receptor antagonists, interacting with membrane‐bound or soluble IL‐6 or IL‐6 receptor. Currently approved IL‐6 receptor antagonists for RA treatment are TCZ and SAR. TCZ intravenous was first approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) [ ] in 2009 and by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2010. Subcutaneous formulation of TCZ was approved following the intravenous formulation of TCZ. SAR is a second IL‐6 receptor antagonist approved for subcutaneous application by the EMA and FDA in 2017. Both drugs are indicated for RA in combination with conventional synthetic DMARDs or as monotherapy [ , , , ]. Although some other drugs acting through IL‐6‐R have been investigated, only TCZ and SAR have gained approval in this indication to date. Additionally, in 2023 FDA announced approval for the first TCZ biosimilar, TCZ‐bavi, for the indication of RA in adult patients. Clinical efficacy of TCZ and SAR in RA has been evaluated in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) as a valuable therapeutic option when other drugs have failed to achieve the expected benefit [ , , , , , , , , ]. Direct comparative RCTs evaluating pain as a primary endpoint are currently lacking; however, insights can be drawn from pharmacodynamic studies, real‐world observational cohorts, and network meta‐analyses (NMAs) [ ]. Saito et al. [ ] conducted a pharmacodynamic study comparing subcutaneous SAR and TCZ in RA patients, demonstrating that SAR achieved a stronger and more sustained inhibition of IL‐6 signaling pathways, as evidenced by greater suppression of phosphorylated STAT3 (pSTAT3) in CD4+ T cells. In a large prospective cohort study utilizing the ANSWER registry in Japan, Onishi et al. In this context, meta‐analyses offer a valuable approach by synthesizing data from multiple RCTs to indirectly compare the relative effectiveness of biologic agents on outcomes closely related to pain, such as tender joint counts and patient global assessments. These analyses provide important insights into the comparative analgesic potential of IL‐6 pathway inhibitors within the broader landscape of RA therapeutics [ ]. A 2024 Bayesian NMA evaluated six RCTs involving 4439 patients with active RA who were either intolerant or had an inadequate response to methotrexate (MTX) [ ]. The study found that all three IL‐6 inhibitors (TCZ, SAR, and olokizumab) were significantly more effective than placebo in achieving ACR20 responses, with TCZ demonstrating the highest probability of being the most effective agent on the basis of surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) scores. SAR ranked second, followed by olokizumab administered every 2 or 4 weeks. The ranking patterns were consistent across ACR50 and ACR70 endpoints. Although pain was not evaluated as a distinct outcome in this analysis, ACR response criteria inherently reflect pain‐related dimensions such as tender joint count and patient global assessment. Therefore, the superior ACR response probability associated with TCZ, followed closely by SAR, may indirectly indicate greater pain relief with these agents relative to olokizumab [ ]. Another NMA evaluated three RCTs, including 1066 patients with active RA, intolerant or inadequately responsive to MTX [ ]. TCZ 8 mg monotherapy demonstrated the highest probability of achieving ACR20 and ACR50 responses, followed by SAR and adalimumab, with sirukumab ranking lowest. Although pain was not a direct outcome, the ACR response criteria incorporate pain‐related measures such as tender joint counts and patient global assessments. Therefore, the superior ACR responses observed with TCZ and SAR likely reflect better pain relief compared to other agents. Safety profiles were comparable, with SAR ranked as the safest biologic by SUCRA, but no significant differences in serious adverse events among treatments [ ]. Taken together, evidence from network‐level comparisons supports the notion that TCZ and SAR are clinically equivalent in their overall ability to reduce pain‐related disease burden in RA. Nevertheless, because of methodological limitations inherent in indirect comparisons—such as variations in trial populations, background therapies, and outcome definitions—caution is warranted in overinterpreting subtle differences in analgesic efficacy between these agents. 6.3 Role in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">TNF</styled-content> Inhibitor Inadequate Responder (<styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">TNF</styled-content>‐<styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">IR</styled-content>) Populations A significant subset of RA patients exhibits inadequate response or loss of efficacy to TNF inhibitors, which complicates disease management and necessitates alternative therapeutic strategies. IL‐6 inhibitors, including TCZ and SAR, have emerged as effective options in this challenging TNF‐IR population [ ]. Head‐to‐head RCTs, most notably the ADACTA trial, have shown that IL‐6 inhibitors provide superior improvement in disease activity and PROs, particularly pain reduction, compared to switching to another TNF inhibitor [ ]. Mechanistically, IL‐6 contributes to pain through neuroimmune sensitization pathways distinct from those targeted by TNF inhibitors, offering a rationale for the efficacy of IL‐6 inhibitors in patients unresponsive to TNF blockade [ ]. Indirect comparisons and NMA reinforce these findings, favoring IL‐6 inhibitors over repeated TNF inhibitor therapy in TNF‐IR populations by effectively reducing persistent inflammation and refractory pain [ ]. These insights emphasize the importance of IL‐6 inhibition as a strategic switch for TNF‐IR patients to optimize pain management and improve QoL in RA. 6.4 Pharmacokinetics of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">IL</styled-content>‐6 Inhibitors and Their Potential Pain Impact The pharmacokinetic profiles of IL‐6 inhibitors, including TCZ and SAR, play a crucial role in their clinical efficacy and potential effects on pain management in RA. Both agents target the IL‐6 receptor but differ in their administration routes, dosing intervals, and serum half‐lives, which may influence their ability to sustain IL‐6 pathway blockade and consequently modulate pain‐related inflammatory processes. TCZ is available in both IV and SC formulations, with an elimination half‐life ranging approximately from 8 to 14 days, depending on dose and route [ ]. The IV form is typically administered every 4 weeks, whereas the SC form is given weekly or biweekly [ ]. SAR, on the other hand, is administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks with a half‐life of approximately 21 days, allowing for sustained receptor occupancy and IL‐6 signaling inhibition [ ]. Sustained suppression of IL‐6 signaling is critical because IL‐6 contributes to peripheral and central sensitization mechanisms involved in RA‐associated pain through modulation of nociceptive neurons and glial cell activation [ ]. Differences in pharmacokinetics may thus affect the consistency of pain control over the dosing interval, with longer half‐life agents potentially offering more stable pain relief. However, clinical evidence directly linking pharmacokinetic differences to superior analgesic outcomes remains limited. Head‐to‐head trials and real‐world studies comparing pain outcomes with pharmacokinetic parameters are warranted to clarify these potential effects. 6.5 <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CRP</styled-content> Levels and Systemic Inflammation: Modifiers of Pain Response CRP remains a widely used biomarker of systemic inflammation in RA and is directly induced by IL‐6 (10) [ ]. Elevated baseline CRP levels have been shown to predict greater clinical and symptomatic response to IL‐6 inhibitors, including improvements in pain and fatigue, which are often poorly correlated with joint swelling or radiographic damage [ ]. Post hoc analyses from ADACTA and MONARCH trials indicated that patients with higher baseline CRP levels (> 10 mg/L) exhibited greater reductions in VAS pain and HAQ scores, suggesting that systemic inflammation may amplify peripheral and central pain pathways via IL‐6‐dependent mechanisms [ , ]. Thus, CRP may act as a surrogate indicator of IL‐6‐mediated nociceptive sensitization, identifying patients most likely to benefit from targeted IL‐6 blockade. Unlike TNF inhibitors, which variably reduce CRP, or JAK inhibitors, which act downstream of IL‐6 signaling, IL‐6 inhibitors directly suppress hepatic CRP production, leading to rapid and robust reductions [ ]. This CRP‐lowering effect may correlate with subjective improvements in well‐being and pain relief, potentially serving as an early marker of therapeutic success. 7 <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">IL</styled-content>‐6 Versus Other <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">RA</styled-content> Treatments for Pain 7.1 Comparative Effectiveness of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">IL</styled-content>‐6 Inhibitors and <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">TNF</styled-content> Inhibitors for Pain Relief TNF inhibitors and IL‐6 inhibitors (especially TCZ) were globally adopted as first‐line biological therapy (in combination with MTX and as a monotherapy) in patients with RA who are refractory to conventional synthetic DMARDs [ ]. In another trial, patients receiving tofacitinib showed disproportionately high remission rates using DAS28CRP, indicating that the drug significantly lowers the synthesis of CRP [ ]. 7.3 Non‐Steroidal Anti‐Inflammatory Drugs (<styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">NSAIDs</styled-content>), Corticosteroids, <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">MTX</styled-content>: Quick Symptom Relief but Limited Chronic Pain Control The mechanisms behind chronic pain in RA remain poorly understood [ ]. Pain may be resistant when RA is in remission and manifests in non‐inflammatory sites [ , ]. Even with significant therapeutic advancements that have reduced synovitis and disease activity, a substantial number of patients still experience pain [ ]. Through their anti‐inflammatory effects, glucocorticoids administered intra‐articularly, orally, or parenterally may offer clinically significant pain reduction in RA [ , ]. Reduced pain can result from either local or systemic effects, and systemic treatment has been shown to provide benefits for up to a year, even though symptoms may return after stopping steroids [ ]. Since inflammation is the primary pain mechanism in RA, DMARDs form the cornerstone of treatment [ ]. With a beginning effect that coincides with the suppression of inflammation over a few weeks, conventional synthetic DMARDs like MTX, sulfasalazine, and leflunomide also lessen joint pain and can be sustained for months [ ]. Therefore, even after using conventional synthetic DMARDs for treatment, pain may continue to be an issue. Although there is a lack of evidence on the management of pain in RA, drugs like NSAIDs, topical capsaicin, and mild opioids, as well as treatments such as joint infiltrations or surgery, are crucial [ ]. NSAIDs reduce pain in RA patients. However, they are not very helpful as a stand‐alone treatment for patients with centrally mediated pain, such as fibromyalgia. We can conclude that by acting on disease activity, TCZ in monotherapy or combination with other conventional synthetic DMARDs indirectly affects pain in patients with RA. 8 Unmet Needs and Future Directions 8.1 Persistent Pain Despite <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">IL</styled-content>‐6 Inhibition: A Clinical Dilemma Despite robust anti‐inflammatory effects and notable improvements in disease activity scores, IL‐6 inhibitors fail to provide adequate pain relief in a subset of RA patients. This phenomenon (persistent pain despite remission or low disease activity) reflects the growing recognition that RA pain is not solely inflammation‐driven. Instead, it is a multidimensional experience shaped by peripheral nociception, central sensitization, psychological burden, and long‐standing neuroimmune dysregulation. Several observational studies have shown that more than 30%–50% of RA patients continue to report moderate‐to‐severe pain despite being classified as in remission by DAS28 or CDAI scores [ , ]. This incongruity reflects the inadequacy of current composite disease activity tools in capturing the true pain burden. Central sensitization, characterized by exaggerated pain responses, altered descending pain modulation, and neuroplastic changes in cortical and subcortical structures, plays a central role in this residual pain [ ]. Since IL‐6 contributes to glial activation, hyperexcitability of dorsal horn neurons, and astrocytic priming, IL‐6 blockade holds theoretical appeal—but it is increasingly clear that its modulation of central pain circuits is not universally sufficient [ ]. Furthermore, coexisting conditions such as fibromyalgia, sleep disorders, mood disturbances, and fatigue often persist under IL‐6 therapy, suggesting that peripheral cytokine suppression alone cannot resolve centrally amplified symptoms [ ]. Pain must therefore be reframed not merely as a symptom of inflammation, but as a neurobehavioral syndrome, requiring targeted and integrative interventions beyond standard biologics. Multidisciplinary care models incorporating cognitive‐behavioral therapy, neuromodulatory pharmacology, physical rehabilitation, and sleep restoration strategies are essential adjuncts. 8.2 Absence of Pain‐Specific Biomarkers: Is <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">IL</styled-content>‐6 a Predictor? This highlights a critical knowledge gap: current serological biomarkers (e.g., CRP, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and IL‐6) reflect inflammatory load, not pain mechanisms. In contrast, pain in RA is often influenced by non‐inflammatory drivers, including disordered sensory processing, neurotransmitter imbalance, cortical maladaptation, and psychological comorbidity. Recent advances in drug design have led to the emergence of dual‐target biologics, which combine inhibition of IL‐6 with other pro‐inflammatory mediators like TNF‐α or IL‐17 [ , ]. These agents, including bispecific nanobodies and fusion proteins, are under early‐phase investigation and may offer synergistic efficacy in both pain and disease control. In addition to dual blockade strategies, targeting IL‐6 trans‐signaling specifically via soluble gp130‐Fc constructs has gained traction. This selective approach aims to block the pathogenic neuroimmune effects of IL‐6 trans‐signaling, whereas preserving classic signaling important for tissue repair and host defense [ ]. Preclinical models suggest that such approaches may yield greater pain modulation with reduced adverse effects. Moreover, combining IL‐6 inhibitors with central neuromodulators is another promising avenue. Serotonin‐norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentinoids, and low‐dose naltrexone have shown benefit in nociplastic pain conditions and may enhance central pain inhibition when used adjunctively with biologics [ ]. Future trials should explore these synergistic pharmacological strategies, particularly in patients with pain‐dominant, inflammation‐negative RA phenotypes. The integration of digital therapeutics, such as mobile‐based cognitive interventions, sleep modulation apps, and virtual pain coping programs, represents a novel adjunctive approach, especially in younger, tech‐enabled patient populations. 8.4 Bridging Mechanistic Understanding With Clinical Trial Design To close the translational gap between mechanistic research and real‐world pain management, clinical trials evaluating IL‐6 inhibitors must evolve. Historically, pain has been treated as a secondary or exploratory endpoint in most RCTs. This has contributed to the underrecognition of analgesic effects and a failure to distinguish mechanistically distinct pain phenotypes. Future trial designs should include [ , , , , ]: Pain‐specific primary endpoints, including VAS, Brief Pain Inventory (BPI), and PROs Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Pain Interference scores Central sensitization assessments, such as QST, fMRI, or CPM paradigms. Stratification by pain phenotype, using validated instruments (e.g., painDETECT, Douleur Neuropathique 4 [DN4], fibromyalgia screening tools) Multimodal outcomes, encompassing fatigue, sleep quality, depression/anxiety scores, and neuroimaging correlates. Incorporating such measures would allow researchers to identify true responders to IL‐6 inhibition for pain, optimize patient selection, and pave the way for biomarker‐informed, individualized pain treatment algorithms. This paradigm shift from inflammation‐centered to mechanism‐guided care could redefine therapeutic success in RA, not just by silencing disease activity, but by truly restoring QoL. 9 Conclusion IL‐6 inhibitors have undergone a distinct analgesic repositioning, emerging as a novel class of disease‐modifying analgesics that extend beyond their traditional anti‐inflammatory role in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) pain management. They target both peripheral and central mechanisms driving chronic pain. Clinical and real‐world studies demonstrate that agents such as TCZ and SAR produce rapid and sustained improvements in PROs, including pain, fatigue, and HRQoL, often outperforming TNF inhibitors in certain populations. IL‐6‐driven sensitization of nociceptors, glial activation, and neuroimmune crosstalk underlie persistent pain in RA—even when inflammation is under control. By uniquely modulating these signaling pathways, IL‐6 inhibitors provide dual benefits—suppressing inflammation while directly alleviating pain—thereby marking a paradigm shift in RA treatment that recognizes pain as a distinct, treatable entity. Despite these advances, a substantial subset of patients continues to suffer from moderate to severe pain, highlighting the multifactorial nature of RA pain, which is characterized by central sensitization, psychological comorbidities, and neuroplastic changes. The lack of validated pain‐specific biomarkers hinders individualized treatment and underscores the need for research that links mechanistic findings to clinical practice. Elevated CRP may predict a better symptomatic response to IL‐6 blockade, but current serologic markers do not reliably reflect pain mechanisms or central amplification. Future development of precision medicine tools for pain phenotyping and response prediction should be a priority. New therapies, including dual‐target biologics and selective IL‐6 trans‐signaling inhibitors, show promise for refractory pain. Integrative, multidisciplinary approaches that combine pharmacologic, behavioral, and digital interventions are essential to fully address the multidimensional burden of RA pain. We need a paradigm shift: away from an inflammation‐centric model to one that recognizes pain as

research that links mechanistic findings to clinical practice. Elevated CRP may predict a better symptomatic response to IL‐6 blockade, but current serologic markers do not reliably reflect pain mechanisms or central amplification. Future development of precision medicine tools for pain phenotyping and response prediction should be a priority. New therapies, including dual‐target biologics and selective IL‐6 trans‐signaling inhibitors, show promise for refractory pain. Integrative, multidisciplinary approaches that combine pharmacologic, behavioral, and digital interventions are essential to fully address the multidimensional burden of RA pain. We need a paradigm shift: away from an inflammation‐centric model to one that recognizes pain as a distinct, multifactorial entity. A better understanding of mechanisms and refined clinical trial design will enable IL‐6 inhibitors to restore patients' quality of life in RA and move beyond suppression of disease activity to true pain relief. documents.title: EULAR recommendations for the management of psoriatic arthritis with pharmacological therapies 2023 update

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Many drugs have become available over the last years in psoriatic arthritis (PsA); trials of new drugs have consistently been positive in terms of the primary outcomes, but it is difficult to obtain an overview of the efficacy and safety of systemic therapies for PsA, including conventional synthetic, biological and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs). WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This systematic literature research (SLR) provides an overview of the efficacy and safety results of: Established DMARDs, trials investigating efficacy of DMARDs on specific domains of PsA (axial, dactylitis, synovitis). Novel biological DMARDs, including inhibitors of IL23-p19 (risankizumab, guselkumab, tildrakizumab), IL17A (izokibep), IL17A/F (bimekizumab). Novel Janus kinase inhibitors, including brepocitinib (JAK1/TYK2), deucravacitinib (TYK2) and upadacitinib (JAK1/JAK2). Studies on treatment tapering and stopping. Safety analyses of observational data investigating established DMARDs on adverse events of special interest (infections, malignancies, cardiovascular and thrombotic events). HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY This SLR informed the 2023 European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology PsA management recommendations task force with the available evidence published since the previous update published in 2019. Introduction Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a chronic inflammatory disease occurring in patients with psoriasis, leading to the typical clinical hallmarks of oligoarthritis or polyarthritis, enthesitis and dactylitis; if left untreated, radiographic damage and, although rare, potentially mutilating joint destruction may occur. Axial disease in PsA was recognised already by Moll and Wright as an important musculoskeletal manifestation, however, many new insights were gained over the past decades, differentiating axial PsA from the manifestations observed in radiographic and non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis, including genetics, pathological findings, clinical symptoms, subsequent radiographic changes and also potential implications for treatment. In 2012, the first European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) management recommendations on pharmacological therapies for PsA were developed, with subsequent updates in 2015 and 2019 . With an increasing depth of understanding immunological pathways of PsA, the body of evidence on the efficacy of new molecules targeting different modes of action (MOAs), such as inhibition of the p19 subunit of interleukin (IL)-23 and IL-17, but also Janus Kinase (JAK) including the tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2) pathway, has significantly increased in recent years. Besides the mere development of new MOAs using established composite endpoints, recent studies also provided evidence on the efficacy of established disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) on specific musculoskeletal manifestations, including synovitis, axial disease and dactylitis. Furthermore, head-to-head trials, comparing different MOAs, as well as conventional synthetic (cs) DMARD regimens and strategic trials, also on tapering strategies, were published. Increasing emphasis on adverse events of DMARD therapies gained attention over the past years due to safety signals identified in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and cardiovascular risk factors receiving a JAKi, namely tofacitinib (TOFA). This may also be important in PsA, given the high prevalence of comorbidities and risk factors, such as obesity, dyslipidaemia, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease and smoking in patients with PsA. This systematic literature research (SLR) was conducted to summarise and update the evidence on pharmacological treatments in PsA since 2019, to inform the EULAR task force developing the 2023 update of the PsA management recommendations. Methods This SLR was conducted according to the EULAR updated standard operating procedures and based on a protocol developed and approved by the task force. To update the evidence from the previous SLR with the data cut on 21 December 2018, articles published in English language between 1 January 2018 and 28 December 2022 were searched by an experienced librarian (JWS) using Medline (PubMed), Embase (OVID version), the Cochrane CENTRAL Register of Controlled Trials (Central) and the abstract archives of the EULAR and American College of Rheumatology (ACR) annual meetings. To prevent missing important publications, we included the year 2018 in the literature search, as manuscripts which carry the date of a specific year might be published with some delay. Like in previous SLRs, conference abstracts from the last 3 years (from 2020 to 2022) were eligible for inclusion. In the case of articles being published after the data cut of the literature search but before the EULAR task force meeting (17 April 2023), fully published manuscripts were eligible to be included only if they had been covered as a conference abstract in the initial systematic search. The search strategies are provided in . 10.1136/ard-2024-225534.supp1 Supplementary data During the first steering committee meeting (21 November 2022), a research protocol was developed. In total, 10 research questions were defined. These research questions covered the areas of the efficacy and safety of already approved DMARDs, safety of JAK inhibitors (JAKi), the efficacy and safety of new molecules, drug–drug interactions, the efficacy of DMARDs on different disease manifestations of PsA, evidence on strategic trials as well as evidence on dose reduction and treatment discontinuation. Based on the research questions, detailed PICO

as a conference abstract in the initial systematic search. The search strategies are provided in . 10.1136/ard-2024-225534.supp1 Supplementary data During the first steering committee meeting (21 November 2022), a research protocol was developed. In total, 10 research questions were defined. These research questions covered the areas of the efficacy and safety of already approved DMARDs, safety of JAK inhibitors (JAKi), the efficacy and safety of new molecules, drug–drug interactions, the efficacy of DMARDs on different disease manifestations of PsA, evidence on strategic trials as well as evidence on dose reduction and treatment discontinuation. Based on the research questions, detailed PICO definitions (population, intervention, control, outcome) were developed. Details on the research questions as well as the PICO definitions are shown in . For efficacy, only randomised controlled trials (RCTs) investigating non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), cs, biological (b) or targeted synthetic (ts) DMARDs in adult patients classified as having PsA were eligible for inclusion. Phase 2 studies were eligible for inclusion, if no phase 3 studies were available, as efficacy but also safety profiles of new molecules, targeting similar pathways as currently licensed drugs, might be informative. For safety, data of identified RCTs as well as long-term extensions studies of RCTs with adequately defined comparator arms (placebo (PBO) or active therapy) were eligible. In addition to RCT safety data (including long-term extensions with adequate comparator arms) also observational studies (including registry analyses, claims data, cohort studies and case–control studies) with adequately defined controls were eligible for inclusion. Patient populations of interest were defined as patients classified as having PsA; patients could be either DMARD-naïve, or with intolerance and/or insufficient response (IR) to csDMARDs, patients who were bDMARD-IR and/or tsDMARD-IR or mixed populations with previous IR to cs-DMARDs or/and bDMARDs; in some studies patients with IR to NSAIDs were also eligible. All interventions of interest are listed in . Efficacy outcomes included composite measures of state (such as Disease Activity Index for Psoriatic Arthritis (DAPSA) or minimal disease activity (MDA)) and of improvement (such as ACR criteria), individual core-set measures of signs and symptoms, patient-reported outcomes (including fatigue, physical function). Safety outcomes included infections (serious infections, herpes zoster (HZ), opportunistic and fungal infections, tuberculosis (Tb)); malignancies; major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs); venous thromboembolic events (VTE); liver disease; gastrointestinal side effects; incidence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), uveitis; depression, suicidal ideation and behaviour ( ). 10% of all titles and abstracts were screened by two researchers (AK and RJOF) with an agreement of 94%. All other titles and abstracts were screened and assessed by one researcher (AK). In the case of any uncertainties, these were discussed with the methodologist (LG). The selected articles were then assessed in full detail for eligibility and data of finally eligible articles were extracted using standardised spreadsheet forms by one researcher (AK) and verified in detail for correctness by the co-methodologist (RJOF). Risk of bias (RoB) assessment was done using the Cochrane Collaborations RoB tool for RCTs (version 2), while the Newcastle-Ottawa scale was utilised for assessing RoB in cohort and case–control studies. Conference abstracts were not assessed for RoB. Due to the high heterogeneity of the finally selected studies, and for the purposes of recommendations, detailed information of each study rather than summary statistics was selected; thus, no meta-analyses were performed and results, including effect sizes derived from safety analyses were taken from the original articles and reported descriptively. Specific adverse events of special interest (AESI) occurring during the double-blind period are reported in detail, while summary estimates derived from long-term extension studies are reported directly following the respective sections on the double-blind period. Results Search results The efficacy search resulted in 3946 articles of which 212 references were selected to be assessed in the detailed article review, resulting in 38 articles describing 30 unique trials eligible for final inclusion in the SLR ( ). A detailed list of studies assessing the efficacy of DMARDs is shown in . provides an overview of the drugs evaluated for efficacy and summarises the main reported efficacy outcomes of the studies included. A total of 19 of the 30 trials (63.3%) were rated as having a low RoB; 7 of 30 trials (23.3%) received a rating of a high RoB—all due to an open-label or single-blinded trial design. Two trials (2/30, 6.6%) had an unclear RoB, both due to insufficient reporting of randomisation sequence generation and allocation concealment methods. One trial was published as a conference abstract only and was not assessed for RoB. All RoB assessments of efficacy studies are provided in , baseline characteristics are presented in , and detailed efficacy results are shown in . For safety, beyond the adverse event profiles presented in the RCT publications already included in the efficacy search, further 2055 references were screened, and 87 articles assessed in detail with 24 studies

due to an open-label or single-blinded trial design. Two trials (2/30, 6.6%) had an unclear RoB, both due to insufficient reporting of randomisation sequence generation and allocation concealment methods. One trial was published as a conference abstract only and was not assessed for RoB. All RoB assessments of efficacy studies are provided in , baseline characteristics are presented in , and detailed efficacy results are shown in . For safety, beyond the adverse event profiles presented in the RCT publications already included in the efficacy search, further 2055 references were screened, and 87 articles assessed in detail with 24 studies finally included ( ). These 24 studies included 9 safety analyses of RCT data (long-term extensions and integrated safety analyses of AESI) as well as 15 observational studies: 8/24 (33.3%) with a low RoB, 1/24 (4.2%) with unclear and 10/24 (37.5%) with a high RoB (5 conference abstracts were not assessed for RoB). Investigations of AESI in RCTs were concerned with influenza, Tb, malignancies and thromboembolic events. Cohort studies investigated serious infections, Tb, solid and haematological malignancies, liver disease, MACEs as well as anxiety and depression ( provides a detailed list of safety studies included). RoB assessments of safety studies are shown in , population characteristics are presented in , with the main safety results shown in . Efficacy of csDMARDs Only one RCT was available: the COMPLETE-PsA trial (low RoB). Patients with a diagnosis of PsA and without concomitant DMARD therapy were randomised to methotrexate (MTX) + leflunomide (LEF) combination therapy (n=39) or MTX+PBO (n=39). MTX+LEF combination therapy was superior to MTX+PBO in achieving the primary outcome (mean change in Psoriatic Arthritis Disease Activity Score; PASDAS) at week 16 (3.1±1.4 vs 3.7±1.3, treatment difference: –0.6, 90% CI –1.0 to −0.1; p=0.025). Nausea and vomiting were more frequent in the MTX+LEF arm (44% vs 28%), as was alanine aminotransferase elevation (31% vs 18%) and altered bowel habits (26% vs 8%). Efficacy of established bDMARDs In total, six placebo-controlled trials investigating approved bDMARDs (one golimumab (GOL), four secukinumab (SEC), one ustekinumab (UST)) with or without concomitant csDMARDs were included (four with low, two with unclear RoB). In GO-DACT (low RoB), MTX monotherapy was compared with MTX+GOL (TNFi) combination therapy in patients naïve to MTX and bDMARD with active dactylitis. An interim analysis at 50% of the planned recruitment suggested favourable results, which led to stopping of patient recruitment. A significantly higher median reduction in the dactylitis severity score at week 24 (primary endpoint) was observed for the MTX+GOL arm (n=21) compared with the MTX+PBO (n=23) arm (−5 vs −2, p=0.026). Assessment of dactylitis via Leeds Dactylitis Index (LDI) also showed significant differences between the arms (−69.4 vs 31.1, p=0.042), while dactylitis remission at week 24 was achieved in 6/20 (30%) vs 4/22 (18%, p=0.477) of patients receiving MTX+GOL vs MTX+PBO, respectively. MRI assessment of dactylitis (secondary exploratory endpoint) showed a significant difference in favour of the MTX+GOL arm (p=0.017). Outcomes assessing other domains besides dactylitis (enthesitis, tender joints, swollen joints, skin, physical function) showed a trend towards better efficacy for the combination therapy arm, without significant differences between the arms. Four trials (two with low RoB, two with unclear RoB) investigated SEC (anti-IL-17A) treatment. CHOICE (unclear RoB) demonstrated superior efficacy of SEC 300 mg (but not SEC 150 mg) every 4 weeks vs PBO (ACR20 at week 16: 51.5% vs 36.9% vs 23.1% for SEC 300 mg (p<0.001), SEC 150 mg (p=0.10) and PBO respectively) in a biological naïve PsA population. The ULTIMATE trial investigated the change of ultrasound synovitis in biological naïve patients treated with SEC 300 mg every 4 weeks, 150 mg every 4 weeks or PBO. The primary endpoint (the ultrasound Global EULAR and OMERACT Synovitis Score mean change from baseline to week 12) was met with higher response rates in SEC (150 mg/300 mg combined group) treated patients vs PBO (−9±0.9 vs −6±0.9; difference: −3 (−6 to –1); one-sided p=0.004). Baraliakos et al. conducted the first RCT investigating DMARD therapy in an axial PsA population. MAXIMISE (low RoB) demonstrated superior efficacy of SEC 300 mg or 150 mg every 4 weeks when compared with PBO, meeting the study’s primary endpoint, ASAS20 response at week 12 (63% vs 66% vs 31%, respectively; p<0.001), as well as demonstrating improvement in MRI imaging (least squares mean difference vs PBO in total Berlin MRI score at week 12 for the entire spine: SEC 300 mg: −0.4±0.1, p<0.01; SEC 150 mg: −0.4±0.1, p<0.05; for the sacroiliac joints: SEC 300 mg −0.5±0.2, p<0.01; SEC 150 mg −0.5±0.2, p<0.01). FUTURE-4 compared SEC 150 mg every 4 weeks with and without loading (ie, SEC 150 mg at weeks 0, 1, 2 and 3) to PBO. Both regimens showed superior efficacy compared with PBO and no meaningful differences between the active treatment arms. The MUST trial

66% vs 31%, respectively; p<0.001), as well as demonstrating improvement in MRI imaging (least squares mean difference vs PBO in total Berlin MRI score at week 12 for the entire spine: SEC 300 mg: −0.4±0.1, p<0.01; SEC 150 mg: −0.4±0.1, p<0.05; for the sacroiliac joints: SEC 300 mg −0.5±0.2, p<0.01; SEC 150 mg −0.5±0.2, p<0.01). FUTURE-4 compared SEC 150 mg every 4 weeks with and without loading (ie, SEC 150 mg at weeks 0, 1, 2 and 3) to PBO. Both regimens showed superior efficacy compared with PBO and no meaningful differences between the active treatment arms. The MUST trial (low RoB) was an investigator initiated, non-inferiority trial, comparing UST (IL-12/23i) + MTX combination therapy (n=88) to UST+PBO (n=85) in PsA patients naïve to UST. While patients received open-label UST treatment, concomitant therapy with either MTX or PBO was masked. At week 24, non-inferiority was observed for the primary outcome (mean DAS28-ESR), further no meaningful differences in secondary outcomes were observed between the groups. Efficacy of targeted synthetic DMARDs Three trials investigating the efficacy of tsDMARDs were included (all low RoB). Inhibition of JAK 1 and 2 via upadacitinib (UPA; 15 mg or 30 mg once daily) was compared with PBO treatment in patients with prior IR to biological DMARDs in SELECT PsA 2 (low RoB). The trial met the primary endpoint, ACR20 at week 12, with significantly higher response rates in UPA-treated patients (UPA 15 mg once daily: 120/211, 56.9%, p<0.001); UPA 30 mg once daily: 139/218, 63.8%; PBO: 51/212, 24.1%, p<0.001). Further, all secondary endpoints were met. Deucravacitinib (DEUC), a selective, oral TYK2 inhibitor, was investigated in a phase 2 double-blind RCT (low RoB) in patients with IR to ≥1 previous NSAID or DMARD therapy. The ACR 20 response at week 16 (primary endpoint) was demonstrated to be significantly higher in DEUC 6 mg once daily (37/70, 52.9%, p=0.013) and DEUC 12 mg once daily (42/67, 62.7%, p<0.001) treated patients compared with PBO (21/66, 31.8%). Higher response rates in improvement of physical function, skin disease as well as enthesitis and dactylitis resolution were observed. Another phase 2 RCT (low RoB) investigated brepocitinib (BREP), an inhibitor of TYK2 and JAK1 with active disease despite previous NSAID or DMARD treatment. BREP 30 mg once daily as well as 60 mg once daily, but not BREP 10 mg once daily, met the primary endpoint (ACR20 at week 16) when compared with PBO treatment (PBO: 29/67, 43.3%; BREP 10 mg once daily: 20/31, 43.4%, p=not significant; BREP 30 mg once daily: 40/60, 66.7%, p=0.0197; BREP 60 mg once daily: 44/59, 74.6%, p=0.0006). Significant differences compared with placebo were also observed in PASI 75/90% responses for BREP 30 mg and 60 mg once daily. Exploratory analyses also showed benefit for BREP-treated patients in achieving MDA and improvement of enthesitis (only for BREP 60 mg once daily) and dactylitis outcomes (only for BREP 10 mg and 60 mg once daily), as well as physical function and fatigue. Head-to-head studies Three head-to-head trials were included (RoB; ). SPIRIT H2H (high RoB), an assessor-blinded, head-to-head trial compared open-label ixekizumab (IXE, IL17Ai) to adalimumab (ADA, TNFi) in bDMARD naïve patients with IR to csDMARDs. The primary endpoint was defined as simultaneous achievement of ACR50 and PASI100 response—assessed for superiority of IXE versus ADA at week 24. Significantly more patients achieved the primary outcome in the IXE group (102/283, 36%, p=0.036) vs ADA (79/283, 27.9%). No significant difference was found between the arms when comparing ACR (20/50/70) response rates, Health Assessment Questionnaire Disability (HAQ-DI) or dactylitis remission (LDI=0). However, comparing PASI75/90/100 results, these showed significantly higher response rates in IXE-treated patients compared with ADA. Other secondary endpoints such as DAPSA remission, MDA, VLDA were also in favour of IXE treatment. The results were maintained until week 54, with a significantly higher proportion of patients achieving a simultaneous ACR50+PASI 100 response (39% vs 26%, p<0.001). In the EXCEED trial (low RoB), bDMARD naïve patients were randomised to SEC 300 mg every 4 weeks or ADA 40 mg every 2 weeks monotherapy in a double-blind manner. The study was powered to show superiority of SEC over ADA in achieving an ACR20% response at week 52. The primary endpoint was not met, with an ACR20 response of 67% vs 62% (p=0.072) for SEC and ADA, respectively. Similar responses were observed between both treatment arms, with the exception of skin outcomes (PASI 75/100) showing higher responses in the SEC arm. Another double-blind head-to-head trial (SELECT-PsA 1, low RoB) compared UPA 15 mg once daily and 30 mg once daily to ADA 40 mg every 2 weeks and PBO treatment in patients with IR to csDMARDs. With ACR 20 response rates at week 12 of 303/429 (70.6%), 332/423 (78.5%), 279/429 (65.0%) and 153/423 (36.2%) for UPA 15 mg once daily, UPA 30 mg

met, with an ACR20 response of 67% vs 62% (p=0.072) for SEC and ADA, respectively. Similar responses were observed between both treatment arms, with the exception of skin outcomes (PASI 75/100) showing higher responses in the SEC arm. Another double-blind head-to-head trial (SELECT-PsA 1, low RoB) compared UPA 15 mg once daily and 30 mg once daily to ADA 40 mg every 2 weeks and PBO treatment in patients with IR to csDMARDs. With ACR 20 response rates at week 12 of 303/429 (70.6%), 332/423 (78.5%), 279/429 (65.0%) and 153/423 (36.2%) for UPA 15 mg once daily, UPA 30 mg once daily, ADA 40 mg every 2 weeks and PBO, all active treatment arms showed superiority compared with placebo (p<0.001). Further, non-inferiority (margin 15%) of both UPA dosages was demonstrated when compared with ADA, while testing for superiority (vs ADA) was only shown for UPA 30 mg once daily (p<0.001) and not for UPA 15 mg once daily (hierarchical testing failed, no p value reported). Radiographic progression at week 24 was low in all active treatment arms. A summary of the trial results is shown in . Efficacy of novel biological DMARDs targeting the p19 subunit of IL23 In total six trials (five with low RoB, one with unclear RoB) were included. Three trials investigated guselkumab (GUS) an IL23-p19 inhibitor. DISCOVER-1 (low RoB) was a phase 3, double-blind RCT investigating patients with and without prior TNFi exposure. The ACR 20% response at week 24 (primary endpoint) was significantly higher in GUS-treated patients compared with placebo (GUS 100 mg every 4 weeks: 76/128, 59%; p<0.001; GUS 100 mg every 8 weeks: 66/127, 52%, p<0.001; PBO: 28/126, 22%). Results in favour of GUS versus PBO, with a trend towards better efficacy in the every 4 weeks arm, were observed also for more stringent outcomes (ACR70 response for GUS 100 mg every 4 weeks: 26/128, 20%; GUS 100 mg every 8 weeks: 15/127, 12%; PBO: 7/126, 6%), physical function, extra articular manifestations like dactylitis, enthesitis and skin disease. Consistent results (not multiplicity corrected) were also shown for patients with or without previous TNFi therapy. In DISCOVER-2 (low RoB) only patients who were naïve to bDMARDs were included. GUS treatment was superior to PBO for ACR20 (GUS 100 mg every 4 weeks: 156/245, 64%, p<0.001; GUS 100 mg every 8 weeks: 159/248, 64%, p<0.001; PBO: 81/246, 33%), however, no clear difference in other outcomes between the two GUS regimens was observed in this study except for radiographic damage progression, with only GUS 100 mg every 4 weeks but not GUS 100 mg every 8 weeks being significantly different versus PBO (Δmodified Sharp van der Heijde Score, mSvDHS: PBO: 0.95; 95% CI: 0.61 to 1.29; GUS 100 mg every 4 weeks: 0.29, −0.05 to 0.63, p=0.011; GUS 100 mg every 8 weeks: 0.52, 0.18 to 0.86, p=0.072). Assessing patients with axial involvement (as defined by the investigator) and evidence of sacroiliitis (MRI or pelvic radiograph as reviewed locally by the respective investigator) showed improvement in GUS-treated patients compared with PBO when assessing axial involvement with the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (GUS 100 mg every 4 weeks, n=95: −2.7, −3.2 to −2.2; GUS 100 mg every 8 weeks, n=83: −2.7, −3.2 to −2.2; PBO: −1.3, −1.8 to −0.9) and the Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (GUS 100 mg every 4 weeks: −1.4, −1.7 to −1.2; GUS 100 mg every 8 weeks: −1.4, −1.7 to −1.2; PBO: −0.7, −0.9 to −0.5) in a pooled post hoc analysis. COSMOS (unclear RoB) investigated GUS 100 mg every 8 weeks compared with PBO in patients who were TNFi-IR, demonstrating superior efficacy of GUS over PBO in achieving the primary endpoint (ACR 20 at week 24: GUS 100 mg every 8 weeks: 84/189, 44.4%, p<0.001; PBO: 19/96, 19.8%) as well as all other secondary endpoints (MDA, DAPSA, physical function, skin disease, enthesitis, dactylitis and fatigue). The efficacy and safety of risankizumab (RIS), another inhibitor of the IL23-p19 subunit, was investigated in two RCTs (both low RoB). In patients with IR to csDMARDs (KEEPsAKE 1), patients were randomised to RIS 150 mg (s.c. at weeks 0, 4 and 16). At week 24 the primary (ACR 20: RIS 150 mg: 277/482, 57.3%, p<0.001; PBO: 161/481, 33.5%) and most secondary endpoints (including MDA, PASI90, enthesitis, dactylitis, fatigue and physical function) except the secondary endpoint of radiographic damage progression (ΔmSvDHS at week 24: RIS 150 mg: 0.23, 0.02 to 0.44; PBO: 0.32, 0.11 to 0.53, p=0.50) were met. Half of the patients included in KEEPsAKE 2 (low RoB) had received bDMARD therapy before the study. Also, this study met its primary (ACR 20 at week 24: RZB 150 mg: 115/224, 51.3%, p<0.001; PBO: 58/219, 26.5%) and all secondary endpoints. A phase 2b study (low RoB) investigated tildrakizumab (TIL; IL23-p19i) 200 mg every 4 weeks or every 12 weeks, 100 mg every 12 weeks and 20 mg every 12 weeks in patients with previous iR to NSAIDs or DMARDs. The primary endpoint was met by all TIL arms compared with PBO (ACR 20 at week 24: TIL response rates ranging from 71%–80%; PBO: 51%), with no clear dose response. Efficacy of novel bDMARDs targeting IL-17 Five trials on novel molecules targeting IL-17 were included (four with low RoB, one conference abstract). Bimekizumab (BKZ), a selective inhibitor of IL17-A and IL17-F was investigated in two placebo-controlled RCTs. BE OPTIMAL (low RoB) investigated patients naïve to bDMARDs against PBO and active control and showed superior efficacy of BKZ 160 mg every 4 weeks over PBO in achieving the primary endpoint (ACR50% response at week 16: BKZ: 189/431, 44%, p<0.001; PBO: 28/281, 10%, reference; ADA: 64/140, 46%, no formal comparison) as well as in reduction of signs and symptoms of other manifestations like skin disease, enthesitis, dactylitis and radiographic damage progression. Similarly, BE COMPLETE showed superior efficacy of BKZ versus PBO in patients with IR to TNFi. Brodalumab (BRO; IL-17-A receptor) was investigated in csDMARD IR patients in AMVISION 1 and 2. After randomisation of 962 patients, both trials were terminated early due to the sponsors’ decision based on observed events of suicidal ideation and behaviour. The primary endpoint (ACR 20 at week 16) was met in both studies, with significantly higher response rates in achieving ACR50/70, PASI responses and resolution of dactylitis/enthesitis. Izokibep (IZO) is an antibody mimetic, a protein with a small molecular size that can inhibit IL17A and is thus a biological DMARD, but not an antibody. It is administered every other week. A 16-week phase 2 study (conference abstract, RoB not assessed) comparing IZO and PBO showed significant results compared with placebo and a slight dose–response relationship (ACR50 at week 16: IZO 40mg every 2 weeks: 20/42, 48%, p<0.001; IZO 80mg every 2 weeks: 24/46, 52%, p<0.001; PBO: 6/43, 13%). Clinically relevant treatment benefits were also observed in enthesitis, dactylitis and nail disease. summarises and updates the evidence on established and new therapies based on the data presented and previous SLRs. Strategic trials Three strategic trials were included in this SLR (all with high RoB due to their open-label design). The NOR-DRUM trial investigated therapeutic infliximab (IFX) dosed based on therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) versus IFX therapy without TDM. In total 411 patients with inflammatory immune-mediated diseases were included in the induction part of the trial, with 42 patients diagnosed with PsA. The primary outcome was the achievement of remission (defined as DAS28-ESR<2.6 for PsA) at week 30, with no difference comparing TDM to standard dosing in the overall analysis, and looking at the PsA subgroup, numerically but not statistically better results for the standard dosing arm (Disease Activity Score 28-ESR<2.6 at week 30: TDM: 5/20, 25%; standard IFX dosing: 12/22, 54.5%; adjusted difference 29.4%, −0.2% to 59.0%). The second part of this trial investigated the sustainment of response in patients who achieved DAS28<2.6 receiving IFX therapy, again comparing TDM to standard dosing. The PsA subgroup showed no clinically meaningful difference in the number of patients with sustained DAS28-ESR<2.6 from weeks 30 to 52 (TDM: 19/28, 67.9%; standard IFX dosing: 16/25, 64.0%; adjusted difference 6.2%, −19.5% to 31.9%). Tapering and withdrawal Four trials investigated treatment tapering and/or stopping (two with high, two with low RoB). Michielsens et al. conducted an open-label non-inferiority TNFi withdrawal trial (high RoB), using a treat-to-target (using PASDAS≤3.2 as target) dose-reduction and withdrawal strategy (n=42) compared with T2T treatment continuation without tapering (n=22) in patients with sustained PASDAS≤3.2. After 12 months, T2T tapering was shown to be non-inferior to a T2T strategy without tapering. Rates of patients in PASDAS LDA were comparable (71% vs 73%) with 24% (T2T with tapering) vs 77% (T2T without tapering) of patients receiving 100% of their daily defined dose and 36% (T2T tapering) vs 0% (no tapering) had stopped any DMARD use. Another open-label study (high RoB) investigated interval prolongation (ie, doubling the dosing interval) and subsequent stopping (after 6 months) of etanercept (ETN) treatment versus ETN continuation. After 6 months, 57% (vs 70%) of PsA patients could double their ETN interval while still remaining in MDA after 6 months. SPIRIT-P3 was a double-blind RCT, in which patients achieving MDA after receiving (open-label) ixekizumab for 36 weeks (158/394, 40%) were randomised to either undergo blinded withdrawal (receiving placebo) or continuation of ixekizumab treatment. The primary endpoint of time to relapse (ie, loss of MDA) until week 64 occurred more rapidly in patients who withdrew ixekizumab (median 22.3 weeks; 16.1 to 28.3, p<0.001). From week 24 to week 104, 67/79 patients (85%) experienced a relapse in the withdrawal group, compared with 30/79 (38%; p<0.001) in the continuation group. After re-treatment, almost all patients reachieved MDA (64/67, 95.5%) with a median time to re-achievement of MDA of 4.1 weeks (95% CI 4.1 to 4.3) in the ixekizumab withdrawal group. A withdrawal substudy (low RoB) of the long-term extension study of TOFA (OPAL Balance) investigated MTX withdrawal in patients receiving TOFA 5 mg BID (two times per day) for at least 24 months as well as MTX (7.5–20 mg/week) for at least 4 weeks. All patients received open-label TOFA and were randomised to either PBO (ie, MTX withdrawal; n=90) or continued MTX background therapy (n=89). After 6 months, no difference was observed in the co-primary endpoints PASDAS (difference 0.09, −0.13 to 0.31) and HAQ-DI (difference 0.03, −0.05 to 0.10). summarises the main results of studies investigating dose reduction and withdrawal.
