Discussion The aim of this SLR was to summarise the evidence regarding efficacy and safety of pharmacological therapies of PsA since the elaboration of the 2019 EULAR PsA management recommendations. Similar to other SLRs, also this SLR has strengths and limitations. Data of trials included were not pooled through meta-analyses, due to high heterogeneity of the trials. Instead, the data were reported descriptively, avoiding (indirect) meta-analytical comparisons between drugs. On the other hand, the literature was fully searched in a systematic manner using predefined criteria. Though 10% of articles were screened in duplicate, each article was analysed for RoB and quality; and the data synthesis was descriptive which avoids overinterpretation. Evidence on the efficacy of csDMARDs and especially MTX was confirmed with clinically meaningful improvements of disease activity observed in the COMPLETE-PsA and GO-DACT trials but is still based on comparisons to other treatment regimens and not to placebo. Combination of MTX with leflunomide provided significantly better efficacy results than MTX monotherapy, however, with substantially higher rates of adverse events. The efficacy of other meanwhile well-established therapies was confirmed and furthermore expanded with trials investigating the efficacy of IL-17 inhibition on specific musculoskeletal domains which showed significant differences compared with placebo treatment for axial disease (MAXIMISE), and synovitis (ULTIMATE), as well as the efficacy of golimumab in combination with MTX (vs MTX monotherapy) on dactylitis (GO-DACT). Several recent trials used more stringent and clinically meaningful efficacy outcomes than the commonly used ACR20% response as a (co)primary efficacy endpoint (ACR50% response at week 16/24). Non-inferiority of ustekinumab monotherapy compared with ustekinumab+MTX combination therapy was shown in the MUST study. Head-to-head comparisons of IL-17i (secukinumab (EXCEED), ixekizumab (SPIRIT-H2H)) compared with TNFi (adalimumab) showed comparable ACR response rates, but better skin responses in IL-17i-treated patients. Two observational studies found higher rates of hospitalised infections in IL-17i-treated patients (compared with TNFi) , while another study did not show an increased risk. No benefit of therapeutic drug monitoring was seen in infliximab-treated PsA patients. Studies investigating molecules targeting the p19 subunit of IL-23 (guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab) as well as new molecules inhibiting IL-17A (izokibep) and IL-17A/F (bimekizumab), showed superior efficacy when compared with placebo across many disease domains (including arthritis, enthesitis, dactylitis, skin and nail disease) as well as improvement of physical function, Fungal infections occurred more frequently in patients receiving IL-17i compared with placebo and TNFi treatment. Only very few cases of fungal infections were observed in IL23-p19i-treated patients. RCTs on novel targeted synthetic DMARDs (brepocitinib (JAK1/TYK2) deucravacitinib (TYK2), upadacitinib (JAK1/2)) showed significantly higher response rates compared with placebo treatment, as well as superiority of UPA 30 mg (but not 15 mg) compared with adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks on the expense of more adverse events. In regard to safety, higher event rates in upadactinib-treated patients of serious infections (including serious and fatal COVID-19 infections), opportunistic infections, and HZ rates were observed, compared with adalimumab, while rates of MACE and VTEs were similar. Also, decreases of haemoglobin levels

few cases of fungal infections were observed in IL23-p19i-treated patients. RCTs on novel targeted synthetic DMARDs (brepocitinib (JAK1/TYK2) deucravacitinib (TYK2), upadacitinib (JAK1/2)) showed significantly higher response rates compared with placebo treatment, as well as superiority of UPA 30 mg (but not 15 mg) compared with adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks on the expense of more adverse events. In regard to safety, higher event rates in upadactinib-treated patients of serious infections (including serious and fatal COVID-19 infections), opportunistic infections, and HZ rates were observed, compared with adalimumab, while rates of MACE and VTEs were similar. Also, decreases of haemoglobin levels were higher in upadactinib-treated patients, while they increased on adalimumab. Increased rates of acne and acneiform rashes were reported in deucravacitinib-treated patients. No trial investigating the efficacy of glucocorticoids was identified, however, observational studies provided evidence of increased adverse event rates (MACE, serious infections, anxiety and depression) in patients treated with systemic glucocorticoids. Trials on strategic tapering (using a T2T approach) were reassuring, showing the potential of successful treatment withdrawal while maintaining disease control, but abrupt treatment cessation led to an elevated risk of disease flares. Results of the safety analysis also highlighted the importance of comorbidities in PsA patients, with higher risks of serious infections especially in patients with one or more comorbidities compared with patients without comorbidities, a higher risk for VTEs in patients with cardiovascular or VTE risk factors. While not associated with any DMARD therapy, an increased risk for non-melanoma skin cancer in PsA patients was observed, as well as an increased all-cause mortality and death from coronary heart disease. This SLR provided the task force with the evolved evidence since 2018 for the 2023 update of the EULAR recommendations on pharmacological management of PsA.

documents.title: EULAR recommendations for womens health and the management of family planning assisted reproduction in SLE and APS

chunks.content: Introduction Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and the antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), SLE-associated or primary APS, affect mostly women of childbearing age. Several ‘unmet needs’ in the management of reproductive and other women's health issues may impact on personal relationships and the decision to have children. Because of earlier recognition of disease and advances in medical treatment, family planning has gained greater importance. Concerns include the effect of pregnancy on maternal disease, the impact of disease activity on fetal health and the safety of medications during pregnancy and breast feeding. Assessment of fertility and feasibility of assisted reproduction techniques (ARTs), use of contraception, management of menopause and surveillance against malignancies need to be addressed. We gathered a multidisciplinary panel of experts to develop evidence-based recommendations on the management of family planning and women's health issues in SLE and/or APS. Methods We followed the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) standardised operating procedures and the Appraisal of Guidelines Research and Evaluation instrument. Through a Delphi-based approach, the committee selected 12 research questions further edited for systematic literature review (see online S1). We searched PubMed using arrays of relevant terms; all English-language publications up to December 2014 were considered. A hand search was also performed in October 2015. Retrieved items were refined based on abstract, full-text content and number of included patients. A detailed presentation of the literature review is given in the online S2. Evidence was categorised based on the design and validity of available studies and the strength of the statements was graded (see online S3). After rounds of discussions, the committee arrived at 12 final statements ( ). Each member rated her/his agreement with each statement. 10.1136/annrheumdis-2016-209770.supp1 Supplementary table Research questions selected for the systematic literature search and keywords used for the Pubmed search 10.1136/annrheumdis-2016-209770.supp2 Supplementary table Summary of the results of systematic literature review 10.1136/annrheumdis-2016-209770.supp3 Supplementary table Level of evidence (LoE) and grade of recommendation (GoR) rating scales Results and discussion Scope and overarching principles These recommendations have been devised with the intention of helping physicians involved in the care of patients with SLE and/or APS and facilitating physician–patient communication. They recognise an implicit need for change in the mindset of health professionals, shifting from caution against pregnancy towards embracement of pregnancy. Accordingly, family planning should be discussed from the first physician–patient encounter and reinforced thereafter. Health professionals should support the patient and her family in their decisions regarding family planning by discussing individual pregnancy risks. Reports on the long-term follow-up of SLE and/or APS offspring are few, showing a reassuring picture on the health conditions of the children, with the exception of some cases of neurodevelopmental alterations that need further confirmation before they are linked to maternal disease. Recommendations Preconception counselling and risk stratification Assessment of risk factors for adverse maternal and fetal outcomes in pregnant women with SLE and/or APS is crucial for preconception counselling and implementing appropriate preventive strategies and patient-tailored monitoring plan before and during pregnancy ( ). In SLE women (with or without APS), prematurity, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia/Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzyme levels, Low Platelet count (HELLP) rates approximate 25–35%, 10–15% and 1.0–1.5%, respectively. In APS women (primary or SLE-related), the respective frequencies approximate 25–35%, 10–20% and 3.0–5.0%. During pregnancy, risk factors associated with adverse outcomes include active/flaring SLE (OR 12.7 for pre-eclampsia/eclampsia; 19.0 for emergency caesarean section; 3.0 for early fetal loss; 5.5 for preterm delivery), active nephritis (OR 5.3 for any adverse maternal outcome), hypertension (OR 4.8–7.3 for pre-eclampsia; relative risk (RR) 1.8 for preterm birth) and use of glucocorticoids, especially at maintenance dose ≥10–20 mg/day of prednisone equivalent (OR 3.5 for preterm birth). Discontinuation of hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is related to an increased risk for SLE exacerbations during pregnancy, and a single placebo-controlled study has suggested a beneficial effect of HCQ on maternal disease activity during pregnancy. Contraceptive measures Women with SLE and/or APS should be counselled about contraception, especially for the prevention of unwanted pregnancies during high disease activity periods and intake of teratogenic drugs. Effective contraceptive measures should be discussed with the patient by weighing the individual risk factors, including general (hypertension, obesity, tobacco use, family history of hormonal-dependent cancers) and disease-related risk factors, particularly disease activity and thrombotic risk (emphasis on antiphospholipid antibodies (aPLs)). The intrauterine device (IUD) can be offered to all patients unless there is a gynaecological contraindication. Copper IUD can be used in any patient, while levonorgestrel-containing IUD should be considered only if the benefits of the released hormone (such as the reduction of excessive menstrual bleeding due to anticoagulation) outweigh the risk of thrombosis. The safety of the combined (oestrogen plus progestin) and progestin-only pill in SLE patients with inactive or stable active SLE and negative aPL has been demonstrated in randomised controlled trials (RCTs). In women with positive aPL ( with or without definite APS ), contraception

antibodies (aPLs)). The intrauterine device (IUD) can be offered to all patients unless there is a gynaecological contraindication. Copper IUD can be used in any patient, while levonorgestrel-containing IUD should be considered only if the benefits of the released hormone (such as the reduction of excessive menstrual bleeding due to anticoagulation) outweigh the risk of thrombosis. The safety of the combined (oestrogen plus progestin) and progestin-only pill in SLE patients with inactive or stable active SLE and negative aPL has been demonstrated in randomised controlled trials (RCTs). In women with positive aPL ( with or without definite APS ), contraception with combined hormones (oral pill, vaginal ring, transdermal patch) should be discouraged. In young women with myocardial infarction or ischaemic stroke and positive lupus anticoagulant, the use of the combined pill increased the risk of arterial events compared with non-users. In fully anticoagulated patients carrying a low-risk aPL profile, oestrogens might be considered for persistent gynaecological disorders not otherwise managed. Compounds containing progestin only (pill, subcutaneous depot injections) are suitable for these women, although their use should be weighed against the risk of thrombosis. Progestin-only emergency contraception is not contraindicated in patients with SLE and/or APS. Risk factors for reduced fertility Few studies have assessed fertility in women with SLE and/or APS by means of hormonal levels (including the anti-Müllerian hormone) or antral follicle count (examined by ultrasound). There is no concrete evidence that the disease per se decreases fertility. However, active disease, especially lupus nephritis, and the use of immunosuppressive drugs may negatively impact on fertility. Alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide (CYC) may cause menstrual irregularities and premature ovarian failure (POF), which is age- and dosage dependent. Similar to the general population, women with SLE and/or APS should be counselled on fertility issues, especially on the negative impact of increasing age (general tendency to postpone childbearing) and certain lifestyle exposures (tobacco use, alcohol consumption). In non-life-threatening disease, treatment with alkylating agents should be balanced against the risk of ovarian dysfunction; rather, less gonadotoxic regimens should be considered. In the presence of multiple risk factors for impaired fertility, ovarian reserve may be assessed in patients with SLE at a younger age than recommended for the general population. Fertility preservation Limited data are available on fertility preservation methods in menstruating women with SLE who require treatment with alkylating agents. Cryopreservation of ovarian tissue or oocytes/embryos are poorly investigated options and require specialised centres, which may not be easily accessible. The most extensively studied method for POF prevention in patients with SLE involves gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues (GnRH-a), with a good safety and efficacy profile (RR 0.12). GnRH-a have been efficacious in patients with cancer. GnRH-a are likely to protect against POF, but there are no data on subsequent pregnancies in patients with SLE. They can cause menopause-like symptoms, which are fully reversible upon discontinuation. A study in childhood-onset patients with SLE aged <21 years suggested that GnRH-a should be administered 22 days before CYC is started or continued. It is nevertheless recommended to start the GnRH-a prior to or concomitantly to initiation of the alkylating agent. Assisted reproduction techniques Evidence on the efficacy and safety of ARTs (ovulation induction therapy and in vitro fertilisation) in women with SLE and/or APS comes from observational studies. Efficacy in terms of pregnancy rate is comparable with that in the general population (up to 30%). ARTs are generally safe if the patient has quiescent disease and is on appropriate antithrombotic treatment if aPL positive. Although it is challenging to define a single protocol, some general measures for prophylaxis in aPL-positive women undergoing ovarian stimulation can be suggested. The type (low-dose aspirin (LDA); low molecular weight heparin (LMWH)) and dosage (prophylactic vs full anticoagulant) of antithrombotic treatment should be recommended as during pregnancy according to the individual risk profile. LDA should be stopped three days before egg retrieval and resumed the following day. Patients taking LMWH should stop it at least 12 hours prior to the procedure and resume it the very same day as long as there is no bleeding. Patients with positive aPL who are not taking LDA during the ovarian stimulation period should start LDA on the day of the embryo transfer, usually in combination with LMWH (which will be continued during pregnancy). Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome can be avoided by milder hormonal stimulation or GnRH antagonist protocol. The use of the ‘natural cycle’ method is another option, although associated with a lower rate of induced pregnancy. The ART induction protocol should be tailored to the individual patient, balancing the safety and effectiveness of the procedure. Predictive biomarkers for maternal disease activity in SLE pregnancy Active SLE during pregnancy, assessed by validated disease activity indices and/or physician global assessment, is associated with increased risk for maternal and/or fetal complications ( see also paragraph on Preconception

combination with LMWH (which will be continued during pregnancy). Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome can be avoided by milder hormonal stimulation or GnRH antagonist protocol. The use of the ‘natural cycle’ method is another option, although associated with a lower rate of induced pregnancy. The ART induction protocol should be tailored to the individual patient, balancing the safety and effectiveness of the procedure. Predictive biomarkers for maternal disease activity in SLE pregnancy Active SLE during pregnancy, assessed by validated disease activity indices and/or physician global assessment, is associated with increased risk for maternal and/or fetal complications ( see also paragraph on Preconception counselling and risk stratification ). Pregnancy-specific SLE activity indices have been developed and validated for their sensitivity in detecting changes in disease activity and diagnosing flares (see online S4). Physicians should be aware of pregnancy physiological changes that can resemble SLE symptoms and signs. Renal activity correlates with adverse pregnancy outcomes and should be monitored by means of urine protein excretion, urine sediment analysis (glomerular haematuria, urinary casts) and serum creatinine level/glomerular filtration rate. Serological markers are useful in monitoring SLE activity and in the differentiation between disease exacerbation (declining serum C3/C4 levels (even within the normal range) and/or increasing anti-double stranded DNA titres) and pre-eclampsia. Smaller increases in serum C3 levels from pregnancy onset to the second or third trimester as well as serological activity (as defined above) that develops during pregnancy, especially in the context of clinical SLE activity, have been associated with increased risk for pregnancy loss, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) and preterm birth. 10.1136/annrheumdis-2016-209770.supp4 Supplementary table Assessment of disease activity during pregnancy in women with SLE Pregnancy monitoring Pregnant women with SLE and/or APS should follow the local protocols applied to pregnancies at high risk for hypertensive disorders and/or placental insufficiency, adjusting the frequency and modality of fetal surveillance according to the maternal and/or fetal status ( ). Fetal surveillance based on biometric and Doppler findings during the third trimester, and particularly the distinction between early and late IUGR, helps to better tailor the time of delivery and reduce perinatal morbidity and mortality. Umbilical and uterine arteries Doppler sonography at 20–24 weeks has good negative predictive value but modest positive predictive value (especially in the absence of biometric signs of fetal growth restriction later in pregnancy) for placental-associated pregnancy disorders such as pre-eclampsia and IUGR. The mode (vaginal vs caesarean section) and timing of delivery are influenced by maternal (hypertensive disorders, anticoagulation status) as well as fetal conditions during pregnancy. Box 1 Ultrasonographic fetal surveillance recommended for pregnant women with systemic lupus erythematosus and/or antiphospholipid syndrome<xref rid="R43" ref-type="bibr">43</xref> <xref rid="R45" ref-type="bibr">45–48</xref> Routine ultrasonographic screening First trimester (11–14 weeks of gestation). Second trimester (with Doppler, preferably at 20–24 weeks of gestation). Supplementary fetal surveillance in the third trimester at monthly intervals Doppler sonography of the umbilical artery, uterine arteries, ductus venosus and middle cerebral artery (particularly in fetuses that have been identified to suffer from early intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), ie, prior to 34 weeks of gestation). In cases of late IUGR (diagnosed after 34 weeks), reduced abdominal circumference growth velocity and/or a reduced cerebroplacental ratio at Doppler investigation was shown to identify fetuses at higher risk of poor perinatal outcome (Doppler of the umbilical artery alone is insufficient). Fetal echocardiography is indicated if there is suspected fetal dysrhythmia or myocarditis, especially in the context of positive maternal anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB antibodies. Other tests (electrocardiogram plus Holter monitor, magnetocardiography, gated-pulsed Doppler technique, velocity-based fetal kinetocardiogram) might detect subtle signs of the development of congenital heart block (CHB), but are not currently recommended as standard practice. CHB associated with anti-Ro/SSA and/or anti-La/SSB has 16% recurrence rate in women with a previously affected child; therefore, it is recommended to perform serial fetal echocardiograms weekly from 16 weeks of gestation onwards. Considering the low risk (0.7–2%) for CHB in women with no previous CHB, it is unclear whether intensive monitoring (weekly/biweekly between 16 and 26 weeks of gestation and less frequently afterwards) in the general population of anti-Ro/La-positive women is cost-effective. Moreover, there is no proven efficacy of protocols for the prevention or treatment of complete CHB. The efficacy of maternal fluorinated steroids has not been established in large cohorts despite initial reports of favourable effects in cases of incomplete CHB, cardiomyopathy, endocardial fibroelastosis and hydrops fetalis. Given the potential of fluorinated steroids for major maternal and fetal side effects, the benefit for fetuses with CHB should be stratified according to the presence of risk factors for adverse outcome. Despite its unproven benefit, the current practice of intensive surveillance for CHB onset in women with positive anti-Ro/SSA and/or anti-La/SSB antibodies and no previous child affected by CHB carries no risk and is well accepted by the mothers. Drugs for prevention and management of SLE flares during pregnancy A single randomised,

despite initial reports of favourable effects in cases of incomplete CHB, cardiomyopathy, endocardial fibroelastosis and hydrops fetalis. Given the potential of fluorinated steroids for major maternal and fetal side effects, the benefit for fetuses with CHB should be stratified according to the presence of risk factors for adverse outcome. Despite its unproven benefit, the current practice of intensive surveillance for CHB onset in women with positive anti-Ro/SSA and/or anti-La/SSB antibodies and no previous child affected by CHB carries no risk and is well accepted by the mothers. Drugs for prevention and management of SLE flares during pregnancy A single randomised, placebo-controlled study as well as non-randomised evidence supports the beneficial role of HCQ in controlling disease activity and preventing flare-ups during pregnancy. Uncontrolled studies suggest an acceptable benefit/risk ratio of oral glucocorticoids, azathioprine and calcineurin inhibitors (ciclosporin A, tacrolimus) in controlling SLE activity during pregnancy. In moderate-to-severe flares, additional modalities can be considered, such as high-dose glucocorticoids (including pulse intravenous therapy), intravenous immunoglobulin and plasmapheresis (may be also used in refractory nephrotic syndrome). CYC should not be administered during the first trimester of pregnancy due to risk for fetal loss (OR 25.5) and should be reserved only for the management of severe, life-threatening or refractory SLE manifestations during the second or third trimester. Available data are not sufficient to evaluate the risk of using belimumab in pregnancy and the drug should not be used unless the benefit outweighs the risk to the fetus. Mycophenolic acid, methotrexate and leflunomide should be avoided due to known or possible teratogenicity. To this end, collaborative groups have developed recommendations for the use of antirheumatic drugs before and during pregnancy and lactation. Adjunct treatment during pregnancy Use of HCQ is recommended in women with SLE preconceptionally and throughout pregnancy. A beneficial role has also been suggested for APS pregnancies, but at present there is insufficient data to recommend its routine use in these patients. HCQ may reduce the odds of CHB occurrence in fetuses exposed to maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies, especially in mothers who already had a child with CHB. The protective role of LDA against preterm and severe pre-eclampsia has been established in non-autoimmune patients. Accordingly, women with SLE at higher risk of pre-eclampsia including those with lupus nephritis or positive aPL will benefit from LDA, preferably given preconceptionally or no later than gestational week 16. In women with definite obstetric APS, combination treatment with LDA and heparin is recommended to decrease the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Statistically significant results have been demonstrated only for unfractionated heparin in RCTs. However, LMWH is preferable for practical reasons and has shown comparable efficacy in prospective studies. Moreover, patients with positive aPL but with no definite classification of APS will benefit from combination therapy if they are considered at moderate to high risk of maternal and fetal complications (see online S5). 10.1136/annrheumdis-2016-209770.supp5 Supplementary table Assessment of disease activity during pregnancy in women with SLE In addition, other regimens such as prednisolone 10 mg/day in the first trimester, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasmapheresis can be considered for selected patients with APS (refractory obstetric APS, women with previous thrombosis, particularly previous or new cerebrovascular events, women with triple aPL positivity). As recommended in the general population, supplementation with calcium, vitamin D and folic acid should be offered to patients with SLE and/or APS, with particular consideration to those with low circulating levels of 25-OH vitamin D in the first trimester of gestation and receiving glucocorticoids and/or heparin for their detrimental effects on bone mass. Menopause and hormone replacement therapy The efficacy and safety of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) (oestrogen plus progestin) in selected patients with SLE has been illustrated in RCTs. Benefit was demonstrated mainly in vasomotor and other hypoestrogenism symptoms. No significantly increased risk of severe lupus exacerbations during 12–24 months of HRT was found, although there was a modest increase in mild-to-moderate flares. There was no increased risk of thrombosis and cardiovascular events, although one of the RCTs included only patients with negative aPL and no previous cardiovascular events and another did not detail the aPL profile. Two cohort studies with long-term follow-up did not report significantly increased risk of cardiovascular events during HRT, although limitations in power and design preclude firm conclusions. Consequently, HRT should be reserved for the management of severe and disabling vasomotor menopausal symptoms, preferably in SLE women with stable/inactive disease and negative aPL. In patients with positive aPL, the use of HRT should be carefully weighed against thrombotic and cardiovascular risks. If menopause symptoms necessitate HRT, it seems reasonable to start it as early as possible to gain an added benefit for bone protection. Optimal duration of HRT in patients with SLE and/or APS is not known, but it seems reasonable to recommend it for the shortest possible duration. Screening for malignancies Women

In patients with positive aPL, the use of HRT should be carefully weighed against thrombotic and cardiovascular risks. If menopause symptoms necessitate HRT, it seems reasonable to start it as early as possible to gain an added benefit for bone protection. Optimal duration of HRT in patients with SLE and/or APS is not known, but it seems reasonable to recommend it for the shortest possible duration. Screening for malignancies Women with SLE are not at increased risk of breast, ovarian and endometrial cancer compared with the general population, and, therefore, should follow the current population screening protocols for these malignancies. Conversely, women with SLE are at higher risk of cervical dysplasia (but not cervical cancer), vagina and vulva cancers, likely associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Women with SLE exposed to immunosuppressive drugs, particularly CYC in a cumulative dose-dependent fashion, are at higher risk of cervical dysplasia. The suggested timing for Papanicolaou (PAP) smear examination would be once a year in heavily immunosuppressed patients or according to the local screening programme in low-risk patients. Subgroups of women with SLE (Caucasian, younger age, lower education, high SLE damage) may be at risk for poorer adherence to screening programmes. HPV vaccination HPV vaccination is currently offered to female and male adolescents for preventing precancerous growths and cancer in the cervix and in the genital area. There are reports of venous thromboembolic events (VTEs) associated with the quadrivalent HPV vaccine. However, of the 31 cases (0.2/100 000 doses vaccine) with documented VTE, 90% had a known risk factor for VTE (APS in two cases). Prospective studies have demonstrated efficacy and safety of HPV vaccination in patients with SLE, although seroconversion rates may be lower in patients receiving steroids and immunosuppressive agents. A few cases of severe SLE flares or abrupt SLE onset after HPV vaccination have been reported. In accordance with the EULAR recommendations, we recommend that HPV vaccination be offered to young women with stable/inactive SLE and/or APS, according to local protocols, with particular caution in those with high-risk aPL profile. The points to consider and the research agenda suggested by the Task Force Members are reported in . Box 2 Points to consider and research agenda Reproductive issues are of paramount importance for women with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and/or antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) and should be addressed on a regular basis by healthcare providers. Preconception counselling and risk stratification are essential for prevention of unwanted complications during pregnancy. The use of hormonal contraception or replacement therapy is feasible but must be weighed against the individual risk of thrombosis. The preservation of fertility should be mentioned while counselling about lifestyles and considered in the treatment choice. Validated protocols for assisted reproduction techniques in patients with SLE and/or APS are needed. Predictive biomarkers for maternal disease activity during SLE pregnancy should be expanded with particular focus on the prediction of pre-eclampsia. Pregnancy monitoring in SLE and/or APS women should aim at the identification of placental insufficiency with fetal growth restriction in order to decide the best timing for delivery and reduce the risk of perinatal morbidity and mortality. The cost-effectiveness of intensive surveillance with fetal echocardiography in patients with positive anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies and no previous child with congenital heart block remains to be established. Hydroxychloroquine is beneficial during pregnancy to reduce the risk of SLE flares and of poor obstetrical outcomes. More data are needed to support its benefit in APS pregnancies. The benefits of cancer surveillance and prevention of gynaecological malignancies need to be communicated to patients.

documents.title: Update of EULAR recommendations for the treatment of systemic sclerosis

chunks.content: Introduction Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by extensive fibrosis, vascular abnormalities, and immune system dysregulation, affecting the skin and various internal organs, including the lungs, heart, gastrointestinal tract and kidneys [ ]. The etiology of SSc remains incompletely understood, although genetic, environmental, and immunological factors are believed to play a role in its pathogenesis [ ]. SSc can be classified into different clinical subsets, typically including diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc) and limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc) [ ], each with distinct clinical features and disease progression patterns. Patients with dcSSc have skin thickening proximal to the elbows or knees, involving areas such as the upper arms, thighs, or trunk, and this subset is often associated with rapid disease progression and significant internal organ involvement. In contrast, patients with lcSSc exhibit skin thickening distal to the elbows or knees and may also have involvement of the face [ , ]. Globally, the epidemiological characteristics of SSc exhibit significant variability. A meta-analysis reported that the overall pooled incidence of SSc ranges from 0.2 to 7.5 per 100,000 person-years, and the prevalence ranges from 3.1 to 144.5 per 100,000 individuals [ ]. The prevalence, clinical manifestations, and disease severity differ across populations from various regions and time periods. For example, African American patients tend to have an earlier disease onset, a more severe disease phenotype, and an increased risk of developing lung fibrosis and scleroderma renal crisis (SRC). Studies from Western countries have extensively characterized the disease characteristics, course, and prognostic factors [ – ]. Common clinical features include Raynaud’s phenomenon, digital ulcers, scleroderma, interstitial lung disease, gastrointestinal complications, and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Serological markers such as anti-topoisomerase I antibodies (Scl-70), anticentromere (ACA), and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are commonly detected and are often associated with specific clinical subsets. However, comprehensive data on the demographic, clinical and treatment characteristics of SSc patients in Asian populations, particularly in China, remain limited. This gap is critical given the potential differences in genetic background, environmental exposures, and healthcare access, which may influence disease presentation and outcomes. The purpose of our study was to systematically describe the demographic, laboratory, and clinical characteristics of SSc patients from a major Chinese tertiary hospital and to provide an overview of the current treatment status in this setting. This study aims to enhance our understanding of SSc in China and offer insights for clinical practice in this field. Methods Study design and population This study was a single-center, retrospective observational study conducted at Peking Union Medical College Hospital (PUMCH) in China. We reviewed the medical records of adult patients (≥ 18 years) diagnosed with SSc between January 2012 and January 2022. The inclusion criteria were patients who met the 1980 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) criteria and/or the 2013 American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism (ACR/EULAR) classification criteria for SSc [ , ]. Exclusion criteria included patients with overlap syndrome. Patients were divided into dcSSc and lcSSc based on the degree of skin involvement [ , ]. The study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of PUMCH (Beijing, China) (I-23PJ495). Informed consent was not relevant as it was a retrospective study. Data collection Data were retrospectively collected from the medical records of patients at the time of their first admission to PUMCH for SSc. The collected data included demographic information, clinical characteristics, laboratory test results, imaging examinations, and treatment details. The parameters assessed were age, gender, ethnicity, body mass index (BMI), disease duration, age at the onset of SSc, age at diagnosis, type of skin involvement, organ involvement, pulmonary function test (PFT) results, pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) on echocardiography, routine blood tests, biochemical examination, urine examinations, creatine kinase (CK), cardiac troponin I (cTnI), N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), hypersensitive C-reactive protein (hsCRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), immunoglobulin (Ig), and anti-nuclear antibody test results. Disease duration was defined as the interval from the onset of the first manifestation attributable to SSc to the first admission. The assessment of cutaneous manifestations and Raynaud’s phenomenon was based on the clinical evaluation documented by the patient’s rheumatologist at the time of admission. PAH was defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure ≥ 25 mmHg, a pulmonary artery wedge pressure ≤ 15 mmHg and a pulmonary vascular resistance > 3 Wood units by right-sided heart catheterization (RHC) or an estimated systolic pulmonary arterial pressure ≥ 40 mmHg on echocardiography when RHC was unavailable [ , ]. Lung fibrosis was assessed by chest X-ray or high-resolution computed tomography [ ]. A restrictive defect was defined as a forced vital capacity (FVC) < 80% of the predicted value on PFTs [ ]. Cardiovascular involvement, assessed by echocardiography and electrocardiography, was defined by the presence of arrhythmia, pericardial effusion, conduction blocks, or diastolic dysfunction [ ].

25 mmHg, a pulmonary artery wedge pressure ≤ 15 mmHg and a pulmonary vascular resistance > 3 Wood units by right-sided heart catheterization (RHC) or an estimated systolic pulmonary arterial pressure ≥ 40 mmHg on echocardiography when RHC was unavailable [ , ]. Lung fibrosis was assessed by chest X-ray or high-resolution computed tomography [ ]. A restrictive defect was defined as a forced vital capacity (FVC) < 80% of the predicted value on PFTs [ ]. Cardiovascular involvement, assessed by echocardiography and electrocardiography, was defined by the presence of arrhythmia, pericardial effusion, conduction blocks, or diastolic dysfunction [ ]. Gastrointestinal involvement was assessed by gastrointestinal endoscopy, manometry, radionuclide studies, or computed tomography. It was defined based on the presence of manifestations including dysphagia, esophageal dilation, gastroesophageal reflux disease, gastrointestinal dysmotility, gastric antral vascular ectasia, or intestinal pseudo-obstruction [ ]. SRC was defined as rapidly progressive renal insufficiency with no other explanation, with or without rapidly progressive hypertension [ , ]. Furthermore, a detailed description of the drug treatment characteristics of SSc patients was provided. We reported the use of immunosuppressive agents and other therapies for SSc-related complications, along with the proportion of usage, drug dosage, and adverse events. Four authors retrieved all data by medical chart review. A standardized data collection form was developed to minimize variability in data extraction and ensure consistent application of the predefined criteria across all four investigators. All investigators participated in a training session using a set of sample medical records to calibrate their understanding and application of the definitions. Any ambiguities encountered during the chart review were resolved through consensus between at least two investigators. Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 25.0 (IBM Corp.). Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic and clinical characteristics. Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile range (IQR), while categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. The Student’s t-test was used to analyze continuous variables with normal distribution, and the Mann-Whitney U test was used to analyze the continuous variables that were not normally distributed. The Chi-square test was used to analyze categorical variables. A univariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with organ system involvement. Variables with a p-value < 0.05 were further included in a multivariate analysis using a binary logistic regression model, employing a backward stepwise selection method. All statistical analyses were conducted based on available data, employing a complete-case analysis approach where cases with missing data for the variables in a given analysis were excluded. A two-sided P value < 0.05 was defined as a statistically significant difference. No adjustment for multiple testing was made in accordance with the descriptive and exploratory nature of this study, as it would have considerably reduced the possibility of identifying clinically significant findings. Consequently, p-values serve as an indicator of potential interest, and readers should interpret the results with the understanding that type I error may be present. Result Patient characteristics This study included a total of 232 SSc patients with an average age of 54.8 ± 12.7 years. Among them, 54.3% were classified as lcSSc and 45.7% as dcSSc. While female patients constituted the majority of the study population, the relative proportion of male patients in the dcSSc group was higher compared to the lcSSc group (sex ratio female/male 2:1 in dcSSc and 5:1 in lcSSc). In terms of ethnicity, the predominant ethnicity among patients was Han nationality, with only 4.7% belonging to ethnic minorities, including Hui, Manchu, Korean, Mongolian, Tujia, and Uyghur. Regarding disease duration, dcSSc patients had a significantly shorter disease course compared to lcSSc patients (5.8 ± 7.3 vs. 10.9 ± 11.3 years, P = 0.000). Additionally, the time from disease onset to diagnosis was markedly shorter in dcSSc patients compared to lcSSc patients (3.2 ± 5.2 vs. 7.9 ± 11.4 years, P = 0.000). All patients exhibited a low BMI (21.5 ± 3.9 kg/m 2 ) (Table ). Laboratory characteristics Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were detected in over 94% of individuals. ACA and anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein (U1RNP) antibodies were more commonly observed in lcSSc, while Scl-70 were more prevalent in dcSSc (36.2%). Only two patients were positive for both ACA and Scl-70 antibodies. Furthermore, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies were exclusively found in the diffuse subtype. A total of 39 patients (30.2%) tested positive for rheumatoid factor (RF). It should be noted that both anti-CCP antibodies and RF tests had high rates of missing data, at 82.3% and 44.4%, respectively. Elevated CK was observed in 18.8% of dcSSc patients, compared to 15.4% in lcSSc, though the difference was not statistically significant ( P = 0.527). both ACA and Scl-70 antibodies. Furthermore, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies were exclusively found in the diffuse subtype. A total of 39 patients (30.2%) tested positive for rheumatoid factor (RF). It should be noted that both anti-CCP antibodies and RF tests had high rates of missing data, at 82.3% and 44.4%, respectively. Elevated CK was observed in 18.8% of dcSSc patients, compared to 15.4% in lcSSc, though the difference was not statistically significant ( P = 0.527). Elevated levels of cTnI were more frequently observed in dcSSc patients (46.6%), which was significantly higher than that in lcSSc patients (31.0%, P = 0.036). A similar pattern was observed with NT-proBNP, which was frequently elevated among SSc patients (79.0%). About one-third of patients with SSc had raised levels of hsCRP. Elevated immunoglobulin levels and decreased complement levels were also observed in SSc patients. Furthermore, proteinuria and elevated serum creatinine were more frequently observed in dcSSc patients compared to lcSSc (Table ). Organ involvement The involvement of different organ systems and the results across various subtypes are presented in detail (see Table ). Skin sclerosis was a prominent feature observed in our patients, with 93.4% of dcSSc patients exhibiting skin thickening compared to 68.3% in lcSSc ( P = 0.000). Raynaud’s phenomenon was a common peripheral vascular involvement in patients with SSc in our study (78.9%). PAH was a common complication in this study, with a high overall prevalence of 44.8%. The lcSSc subset had a slightly higher occurrence of PAH (47.5%) compared to the dcSSc subset (41.6%). Additionally, lcSSc patients had significantly higher PASP levels (51.9 ± 23.0 mmHg) compared to dcSSc patients (40.8 ± 16.0 mmHg, P = 0.001). Among PAH patients, the mean PASP was 58.7 ± 18.5 mmHg (data not shown). Pulmonary fibrosis was more common in dcSSc (22.9%) than in lcSSc (17.7%). PFT was performed in about 48% of the patients. The mean ± SD of forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), FVC, FEV1/FVC ratio, and diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) on PFT were 75.7 ± 17.3, 79.7 ± 18.1, 81.8 ± 11.1, and 53.3 ± 18.0, respectively. Cardiac complications were reported at similar frequencies in both the dcSSc and lcSSc subsets. Conduction blocks had the lowest incidence among the cardiac complications, occurring in 7.9% of dcSSc patients and 2.5% of lcSSc patients. Gastrointestinal involvement was also common, with esophageal involvement being the most frequent, occurring in 56.5% of patients. Stomach involvement occurred in 32.8% of patients and intestinal involvement in 19.0%. SRC was significantly more frequent in dcSSc patients (26.4%) compared to lcSSc (7.1%, P = 0.000). Treatment Treatment data were available from a total of 228 individuals. The medication characteristics and median dosages for SSc patients are summarized in Table . A high proportion of patients (85.1%) received glucocorticoids, with a median daily dose of 27.5 mg. Among other immunosuppressive agents, 51.8% and 11.0% of patients were treated with cyclophosphamide and hydroxychloroquine, respectively, with median doses of 400 mg/week and 400 mg/day. The proportion of dcSSc patients receiving glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide was significantly higher than that of lcSSc patients. Among the 228 patients, 150 (65.8%) received a combination of two medications, while 20 (8.8%) received three medications. Among the other medications, the most frequently prescribed were proton pump inhibitors (PPI) (64.5%), diuretics (28.1%), calcium channel blockers(CCB) (24.6%), traditional Chinese medicine (23.7%), and angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibitors (23.0%). Additionally, 14.0% of patients in this study were treated with endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs), including ambrisentan, bosentan, and macitentan, and 15.4% received phosphodiesterases-5 inhibitors (sildenafil and tadalafil). 12 patients were treated with a combination of ERAs and phosphodiesterases-5 inhibitors. These vasodilators, which are crucial for managing PAH, were more frequently prescribed to lcSSc patients compared to dcSSc patients. Traditional Chinese medicines, including tripterygium glycosides, total glycosides of paeony, and other herbal formulations, were used in 23.7% of patients. Among these, tripterygium glycosides was the most frequently prescribed agent (48.1%). Furthermore, traditional Chinese medicines was predominantly used as part of combination therapy, with 88.9% of users concurrently receiving conventional immunosuppressants such as cyclophosphamide or glucocorticoids. There were 10 cases of drug-related adverse reactions reported in this study. Of these, four cases involved cyclophosphamide-related pancytopenia, three cases were linked to tripterygium glycosides, affecting the hematologic and gastrointestinal systems, and the remaining three cases involved sildenafil-related low-grade fever, methotrexate-related liver injury, and pirfenidone allergy. All of the adverse reactions improved following drug discontinuation or reduction. All of the adverse reactions improved following drug discontinuation or reduction. Multivariate analysis of disease determinants Based on the binary logistic regression analysis, the associations between complications in different organ systems and various factors were identified. Table presents the results that showed statistically significant differences. The presence of ACA antibodies was significantly associated with a decreased risk of skin sclerosis (OR = 0.361, 95% CI: 0.158–0.827). Elevated NT-proBNP was significantly associated with increased risk of PAH (OR = 12.539, 95% CI: 2.660–57.429.660.429.429) and pericardial effusion (OR = 2.796, 95% CI: 1.114–7.015). High levels of hsCRP were also linked to greater odds of developing PAH (OR = 3.239, 95% CI: 1.137–7.653). Furthermore, skin sclerosis was significantly associated with stomach involvement (OR = 3.122, 95% CI: 1.183–8.239), and lower BMI was also found to be related to gastrointestinal involvement. Discussion This study presents a comprehensive analysis of SSc patients from a Chinese national tertiary referral center, focusing on demographic, clinical, and treatment characteristics. Our findings provide important insights into the patterns of SSc in this population. Our study offers a comprehensive description of this SSc population, as it addresses a wide range of clinical aspects. In this study, female patients accounted for 76.7%, a proportion similar to that reported in Belgium [ ]. The relatively higher proportion of males in the dcSSc group compared to the lcSSc group is also consistent with previous reports. However, the overall proportion of male patients, particularly in the dcSSc group, is higher than that in other large studies [ – ]. This may be explained by several factors. Clinically, the high proportion of dcSSc in our cohort is a key factor, as males are more prone to this subtype [ ]. Serologically, this is supported by the strong association between male sex and Scl-70 (an antibody linked to dcSSc). Biologically, hormonal differences may contribute, as preclinical and clinical evidence suggests a role for estrogens and androgens [ ]. Furthermore, the single-center design at a tertiary hospital may have introduced referral bias, favoring more severe disease. Additionally, the shorter disease duration and time to diagnosis in dcSSc versus lcSSc further reflect its more aggressive nature and earlier recognition. Serologically, ACA and Scl-70 are typically linked to lcSSc and dcSSc, respectively. However, our study also found an association between anti-U1RNP antibodies and lcSSc, consistent with prior reports [ ]. This antibody is also known to be the most common autoantibody in SSc-overlap syndromes and is associated with younger age at onset [ ]. Additionally, notable regional differences in antibody frequencies have been reported. Our Scl-70 prevalence is higher than that in some Western cohorts but comparable to Germany (27.6%) and lower than France (35.0%) [ , – ]. Within Asia, Scl-70 rates vary substantially, with our prevalence falling below that of India (61.3%), South Korea (42.5%), and Malaysia (32.3%) but above Japan (23.3%) [ , – ]. Conversely, our ACA frequency is lower than in most European cohorts but higher than in France (18.0%), while within Asia, it is higher than in India (14.2%) and Malaysia (16.2%) but lower than in South Korea (25.5%) and Japan (36.1%) [ , , , , – ]. These serological patterns only partially align with the reported higher Scl-70 and lower ACA prevalence among Asian SSc patients [ ], indicating the need for further research on regional antibody epidemiology and clinical differences. Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies were not analyzed due to data limitations. Skin involvement is the most common feature among patients with SSc, particularly in those with dcSSc. Additionally, the incidence of pulmonary fibrosis, renal crisis, and cardiac complications is higher in the dcSSc subgroup, supported by corresponding biomarker elevations. The lower prevalence of lung fibrosis compared to other Asian studies may relate to our lower Scl-70 frequency, which is strongly linked to this complication [ – ]. Previous studies have reported that the occurrence of SRC ranges from 1% to 14%, depending on geographical location, with higher rates observed in Australia, the United States, and the United Kingdom, similar to the incidence observed in our study [ ]. Conversely, PAH was considered more common in lcSSc [ ], consistent with our findings; however, recent cohorts suggest its prevalence in dcSSc is higher than historically recognized [ , , ], warranting further investigation. Multivariate analysis demonstrated a significant association between stomach involvement and skin sclerosis. Walker et al. reported that severe gastrointestinal involvement was independently associated with skin involvement but was unrelated to antibody status [ , ]. This supports the role of fibrotic mechanisms in gastrointestinal pathogenesis [ , ], underscoring the need to screen patients with significant skin involvement for gastrointestinal complications. Multivariate analysis demonstrated a significant association between stomach involvement and skin sclerosis. Walker et al. reported that severe gastrointestinal involvement was independently associated with skin involvement but was unrelated to antibody status [ , ]. This supports the role of fibrotic mechanisms in gastrointestinal pathogenesis [ , ], underscoring the need to screen patients with significant skin involvement for gastrointestinal complications. Furthermore, low complement levels have been shown to be associated with SSc patients who have overlap diseases and are significantly correlated with lower BMI, which indicates more active and severe gastrointestinal involvement [ , ]. Our analysis conversely linked low complement 4 levels and high BMI to reduced risk of esophageal involvement. This discrepancy may be attributed to various factors, including differences in study design and statistical methods. Moreover, our finding of a strong association between elevated NT-proBNP and PAH risk supports prior evidence, which identifies it both as an independent predictor for PAH and as a marker closely related to hemodynamics in SSc-PAH patients [ , ], despite the wide confidence interval likely reflecting our sample size limitations. Similarly, elevated hsCRP was moderately but significantly associated with PAH, reinforcing the link between systemic inflammation and vascular complications. This is supported by evidence tying CRP to SSc-PAH, progressive fibrosis, and decreased survival [ – ], as well as to increased oxidative stress in SSc [ ], collectively suggesting its potential value as a clinical indicator. SRC was significantly correlated with elevated cTnI. This correlation may stem from the high incidence of cardiac complications in SRC, where severe cases can present with seizures or symptomatic pericardial involvement [ , ]. A retrospective study involving 19 SRC patients found that NT-proBNP levels > 360 pmol/L were highly correlated with the need for dialysis [ ]. However, no studies have yet confirmed whether cTnI can serve as a predictive marker for SRC. Collectively, these findings emphasize the need to identify reliable biomarkers for disease progression and prognosis in SSc. Additionally, our estimates for less frequent outcomes should be interpreted with caution due to the limited number of events. In terms of pharmacotherapy, the higher use of glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide in dcSSc suggests that clinicians are more likely to adopt intensive immunosuppressive regimens in response to the rapid progression and more severe organ involvement in this group. Our high glucocorticoid usage aligns with a Singaporean cohort [ ] but exceeds some Western reports [ , ]. Their use in SSc, however, remains controversial. Although expert consensus includes them as part of the management strategy for interstitial lung disease, diffuse cutaneous disease, or musculoskeletal involvement [ ], contemporary guidelines unanimously recommend employing the lowest effective dose with close monitoring of blood pressure and renal function, considering the potential risk of SRC [ , ]. The utilization pattern observed in our study may reflect a clinical balance between the need to control active inflammation and long-term risks. Substantial variation in glucocorticoid usage rates across centers (6.9% to 77%) [ ] underscores the lack of consensus and the need for more judicious, evidence-based strategy. Beyond glucocorticoids, the predominance of cyclophosphamide use in diffuse patients is supported by other studies, though its lower survival rates compared to methotrexate [ , ] may reflect treatment allocation bias in patients with greater organ burden. Conversely, methotrexate was used infrequently in our population despite guideline recommendations for skin fibrosis [ , , ]. This discrepancy is well explained by its typical reservation for milder disease presentations—a practice directly supported by the pivotal trial [ ], which demonstrated benefit primarily in patients with limited SSc and mild organ involvement, a profile distinct from our overall severely affected study population with significant visceral organ involvement. The higher frequency of vasodilator use in lcSSc patients is consistent with the observation of elevated PASP levels and an increased risk of PAH in this population. Tripterygium glycosides, a traditional Chinese medicine, is widely used in clinical practice as a supplementary treatment for SSc due to its immunomodulatory properties and favorable cost-effectiveness. Study from China have demonstrated that tripterygium glycosides, when used as maintenance therapy, significantly improves FVC and FVC% ( P < 0.05) [ ], and survival analysis has shown a protective effect on mortality in SSc patients [ ]. The role of traditional Chinese medicine in SSc warrants further investigation. Systematic reviews have reported tripterygium glycosides-associated adverse effects, including menstrual irregularities, gastrointestinal symptoms, cytopenia, and elevated transaminases, which are consistent with the adverse reactions observed in our patients [ , ]. Notably, all adverse drug reactions in this study were actively reported and documented; however, we cannot rule out

cost-effectiveness. Study from China have demonstrated that tripterygium glycosides, when used as maintenance therapy, significantly improves FVC and FVC% ( P < 0.05) [ ], and survival analysis has shown a protective effect on mortality in SSc patients [ ]. The role of traditional Chinese medicine in SSc warrants further investigation. Systematic reviews have reported tripterygium glycosides-associated adverse effects, including menstrual irregularities, gastrointestinal symptoms, cytopenia, and elevated transaminases, which are consistent with the adverse reactions observed in our patients [ , ]. Notably, all adverse drug reactions in this study were actively reported and documented; however, we cannot rule out the possibility of unreported reactions. This study has several limitations. First, its retrospective design limited data completeness, with some variables (e.g., anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies) entirely absent and others (e.g., pulmonary function tests) having high missing rates, which may reduce the comprehensiveness of phenotypic characterization and statistical power for related analyses. Similarly, the exact onset dates of non–Raynaud’s phenomenon were often not documented or were unreliable due to recall bias. Therefore, we used the more readily ascertainable time point of the first SSc-attributable manifestation, which included Raynaud’s phenomenon. Second, although we defined PAH by the gold standard of RHC whenever possible, this procedure was not universally performed in our clinical practice due to its invasive nature and cost, which led to reluctance among a majority of patients. Consequently, for patients who did not undergo RHC, the PASP measured by echocardiography was used as a surrogate modality for defining PAH. Third, our cohort was defined using the 1980 ACR and/or the 2013 ACR/EULAR criteria, an approach shared by other retrospective studies [ , , ]. However, as the 1980 criteria were developed using patients with longstanding SSc and are known to exclude a proportion of patients with early or limited cutaneous disease, and given that our study did not specifically include other subtypes such as SSc sine scleroderma, the extrapolation of our findings to the entire SSc spectrum may be limited. Nevertheless, our data robustly support the distinction between lcSSc and dcSSc. Lastly, this was a retrospective study from a single national tertiary referral center, which may introduce referral bias by overrepresenting patients with more severe disease, and the data on treatment and follow-up were not as comprehensive as in prospective studies. Future large-scale prospective studies are necessary to determine the optimal treatment strategies for different SSc subgroups. Conclusion This study provides a comprehensive overview of the demographic, clinical, laboratory characteristics and drug treatment of patients with SSc treated at a major Chinese tertiary hospital. In our study, patients often present with multi-organ involvement. The widespread use of immunosuppressants and adjunctive therapies, such as traditional Chinese medicine, underscores the need for more precise pharmacological strategies in managing SSc. Additionally, our study has confirmed associations between specific biomarkers and SSc complications, providing a basis for early identification of high-risk patients. Further studies are warranted to elucidate the clinical utility of these biomarkers.
