As such, concerns regarding COVID-19 can be met, and therapy continuation will be guaranteed. The statistician will be blinded to the allocation of the treatment groups. Data collection Assessments will be performed: T 0 : within 1 week after randomisation (baseline). T 1 : at week 2–3 (pretreatment and post-treatment session) during intervention. T 2 : at week 10–11 (pretreatment and post-treatment session) during intervention. T 3 : after finishing intervention (minimum 48 hours after last treatment session) (week 13). T 4 : 13 weeks after intervention (week 26). T 5 : 52 weeks after intervention (week 64). A detailed overview of the study timeline can be found in and . 10.1136/bmjopen-2023-074258.supp2 Supplementary data Data management Biomarkers will be measured using ultra-senstitivity ELISA and/or multiplex (Luminex platform) assays. Statistical methods All data analyses will be performed by a statistical consultant at the Interfaculty Center Data processing and Statistics. A multiple mediators model will be estimated with a path-analysis using structural equation models. The analysis proceeds in three steps as suggested by Baron and Kenny. In step 1, the direct effects of the manipulated variables on the outcome will be assessed ( —path 1). In step 2, the effect of these variables on the mediators (inflammation/endogenous analgesia) will be assessed ( —paths 2 and 4). In step 3, the combined effect of both the manipulated variables and the mediators on the outcome ( —paths 1, 3 and 1, 5) will be assessed. It will also be explored whether both mediators are related ( —path 6). The importance of the explanatory outcomes will be investigated by a multiple regression analysis. Patient and public involvement During the preparation of the research, we made inquiries with a national patient group (Reumanet) who identified barriers for implementing the interventions. Ethics and dissemination This study has ethics approval (Universitair Ziekenhuis Brussel; B.U.N. 143201941843). The research team are committed to full disclosure of the results of the trial. Findings will be reported in accordance with Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials guidelines. Given the multitude of outcome parameters, results will be divided over several papers. The funder will take no role in the analysis or interpretation of trial results. Supplementary Material Reviewer comments Author's manuscript

documents.title: 2018 update of the EULAR recommendations for the management of hand osteoarthritis

chunks.content: Osteoarthritis of the hands (HOA) is a common, painful and disabling musculoskeletal disorder, with prevalence increasing with age. Clinically, it manifests with bony enlargements, deformities of the hand joints, and occasionally soft tissue swelling. HOA significantly reduces quality of life, causing hand pain, stiffness, functional limitations, and decreased grip strength. As no causal pharmacological intervention exists, treatment focuses on symptom management and involves both pharmacological and non-pharmacological approaches. , Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the recommended first-line pharmacological therapy. , However, NSAIDs should only be used for a limited duration with attention to the risk-benefit ratio. NSAIDs are associated with potentially life-threatening side effects, particularly in the gastrointestinal and cardiovascular systems, especially in older patients. , Consequently, NSAID use is often restricted, prompting patients with HOA to seek alternative treatment options. While non-pharmacological therapies are internationally recommended, evidence supporting some of these interventions remains limited. , In this context, the previously recommended balneotherapy for HOA , was withdrawn in 2018 by the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR), citing its reliance on expert opinion and extrapolation from studies on hip and knee osteoarthritis. However, balneotherapy with thermal mineral water is used since ancient times to relief symptoms of osteoarthritis (OA). Nowadays, balneotherapy for rheumatic diseases has a robust scientific foundation, supported by controlled studies. - Recent findings reveal intriguing molecular effects of balneotherapy on the cytokine milieu and the immune system. , This is of particular interest as HOA displays inflammatory findings. In addition, many studies investigating balneotherapy and/or thermotherapy suffer from methodological limitations, highlighting the need for new clinical trials employing more rigorous study designs and statistical analyses. Therefore, we conducted a randomized, prospective, double-blind, sham-controlled study with a 12-week follow-up to evaluate the effects of serial Bad Nauheim thermal brine hand baths in patients with painful HOA. Materials and methods Ethical approval was granted by the ethics committee of the Faculty of Medicine of the Justus-Liebig-University Gießen, Germany (vote no. 56/22). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. All the examinations comply with the Helsinki Declaration. We conducted a prospective, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled, monocentric trial with a parallel design and a 1:1 allocation ratio to assess effects of serial thermal brine hand baths (thermal) vs. tap water hand baths (tap) on HOA. Two care providers were blinded to group assignments and delivered interventions in both groups. No changes to the methods, including eligibility criteria, were made after the trial commenced. For inclusion patients with bilateral painful HOA had to meet the 1990 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) classification criteria. Eligible patients were required to have a baseline pain level >30 mm on the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and radiographic evidence of hand osteoarthritis in posteroanterior X-ray projection, classified as Kellgren and Lawrence grade ≥2. Patients were excluded if they were taking analgesic therapy (NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, metamizole, opioids), steroids, glucosamine medication or received physical therapy for HOA 12 weeks prior to study start. Patients had to have no prior therapy with hand-bath (ever). Furthermore, patients were excluded if they had (secondary) HOA due to various inflammatory rheumatic diseases or active HOA (acute inflammation at study start), trauma or open wounds. Patients with diabetes, vasoactive medication, trophic skin disorders, concomitant vascular disease, sensory deficits (polyneuropathy), Raynaud disease or smokers were excluded. The study was conducted at Campus Kerckhoff, Justus-Liebig-University Gießen, Dept. of Rheumatology, Clinical Immunology, Osteology and Physical Medicine, Bad Nauheim, Germany. All data was collected at Sprudelhof Bad Nauheim, where interventions were delivered. The intervention group (IG) received serial thermal, the control group (CG) received a sham intervention consisting of serial tap. Both groups received 6 hand baths in 3 weeks with 2 hand baths per week. Each hand bath had a duration of 15 min. The temperature of 25 °C was the same for both thermal brine and tap water to ensure blinding. Temperature was chosen based on the natural temperature of the thermal brine, which was not heated artificially. Thermal used Bad Nauheimer thermal brine (sodium chloride hydrogen carbonate acidulant: CO 2 2250 mg/L, HCO 1068 mg/L, Ca 2+ 1370 mg/L, Cl - 18100 mg/L, Na + 10600 mg/L, test report Institut Fresenius No. 6060087, 09/2022, Bad Homburg, Germany). Tap used local tap water (CO2 n.a. mg/L, HCO 3 176 mg/L, Ca2+ 62.3 mg/L, Cl- 70.8 mg/L, Na+ 32.8 mg/L, Prüfbericht 250000989, Stadtwerke Bad Nauheim GmbH). Interventions were administered after a 20-minute acclimatization period (pre-rest phase) in a quiet and air-conditioned room at Sprudelhof Bad Nauheim (23 °C). Both thermal and tap were prepared according to protocol in identical bowls in a designated preparation room by unblinded study staff before being brought to the study room. The hand baths were covered, ensuring that both care providers and the patients remained blinded to the treatment allocation. Before immersion an optical sensor was attached to the end phalanx of

HCO 3 176 mg/L, Ca2+ 62.3 mg/L, Cl- 70.8 mg/L, Na+ 32.8 mg/L, Prüfbericht 250000989, Stadtwerke Bad Nauheim GmbH). Interventions were administered after a 20-minute acclimatization period (pre-rest phase) in a quiet and air-conditioned room at Sprudelhof Bad Nauheim (23 °C). Both thermal and tap were prepared according to protocol in identical bowls in a designated preparation room by unblinded study staff before being brought to the study room. The hand baths were covered, ensuring that both care providers and the patients remained blinded to the treatment allocation. Before immersion an optical sensor was attached to the end phalanx of the index finger of the utility hand for assessing microcirculation (by O2C). Since effects of thermal baths on skin circulation may vary at different times of the day, the immersions were always carried out in the period from 9 to 12 a.m. (Monday to Friday). Interventions were administered by protocol to enhance adherence of care providers and participants. Due to the COVID pandemic and regulatory requirements only one patient at a time received the intervention. Patients did not meet. Primary outcome of this trial was pain relief after the intervention period. Pain relief was defined as the change from baseline in resting pain intensity after intervention. Pain (primarily at rest and secondary during activities of daily life within the last 48 hours) was assessed on a standardized VAS (0 mm=no pain, 100 mm=worst possible pain) before and after each intervention. In addition, follow-up assessments evaluated pain 4 weeks (w4) and 12 weeks (w12) after the intervention period. A change in pain greater than 10 mm on VAS in general and 20 mm on VAS measuring chronic musculoskeletal pain intensity is defined as the minimal clinically important difference (MCID). Secondary outcomes were changes from baseline 1) in the Australian/Canadian Osteoarthritis Hand Index (AUSCAN), 2) grip strength, 3) microcirculation and 4) patient satisfaction as well as 5) number and manner of adverse events. All secondary outcomes were assessed at every intervention and at both follow-up visits (w4 and w12). The AUSCAN is a validated, self-reported outcome measure specifically designed to assess symptoms and functional limitations HOA. It comprises three subscales: pain (5 items), stiffness (1 item), and physical function (9 items). Participants rate each item on a Likert scale ( e.g. , 0=no symptoms, 4=extreme symptoms), with higher scores indicating greater severity. The total score is the sum of the subscales, providing a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of HOA on daily life. Grip strength was assessed using an electronic hand dynamometer (Model No.: EH101, manufacturer: Kuptone, MAX 90 kg), a device comparable to the Jamar Dynamometer, with high reliability and validity demonstrated in studies (interrater reliability: r=0.97; test-retest reliability: r=0.9). , The device measures isometric hand muscle strength in kilograms. Participants were instructed to grip the device with maximum effort. Initially, a “warm-up phase” consisting of three measurements per each hand was conducted, followed by three additional measurements, with the mean value calculated to enhance re-test reliability. This method provides a quantitative evaluation of hand function and strength, commonly used in HOA research. , Microcirculation and tissue oxygenation were assessed using the O2C (Oxygen to See) device (LEA Medical Technology, Gießen, Germany), a validated method combining photospectrometry and laser Doppler flowmetry. , An optical sensor placed on the index finger of the dominant hand measured three parameters without artifacts: microvascular blood flow (arbitrary units, AU), postcapillary oxygen saturation (SO 2 , %), and relative hemoglobin concentration (rHb, AU), representing vascular density and microvascular filling. This approach provides a comprehensive evaluation of functional microcirculatory parameters. , , - In addition, Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF), a key regulator of angiogenesis and new blood vessel formation was measured in serum samples collected before the first and after the last (6th) hand immersion ensuring consistent timing to control for circadian variation. Serum was quickly delivered to the laboratory to be centrifuged at 3,500 rpm at 15 °C for 10 minutes, stored at -80 °C, and analyzed using Quantikine ® ELISAs (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA; range: 31.3-2000 pg/mL) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Patient satisfaction regarding the effectiveness and importance of the treatment was assessed after the final (6th) hand immersion using a Likert Scale, a validated psychometric tool. , Participants rated their experience on predefined statements: effectiveness (“not effective” to “very effective”) and importance (“not important” to “very important”), providing a structured evaluation of their perceived treatment outcomes. There was no change in trial outcomes after the trial commenced. The sample size was determined to be 25 patients per group with a drop-out rate of 20% to demonstrate the superiority (difference of 15 mm VAS) of thermal compared to tap based on the primary outcome (change in pain levels). Effect sizes were extrapolated as no comparable trials are published. Calculations were performed using nQuery

a validated psychometric tool. , Participants rated their experience on predefined statements: effectiveness (“not effective” to “very effective”) and importance (“not important” to “very important”), providing a structured evaluation of their perceived treatment outcomes. There was no change in trial outcomes after the trial commenced. The sample size was determined to be 25 patients per group with a drop-out rate of 20% to demonstrate the superiority (difference of 15 mm VAS) of thermal compared to tap based on the primary outcome (change in pain levels). Effect sizes were extrapolated as no comparable trials are published. Calculations were performed using nQuery 8.4.1. Randomization was applied by a random allocation sequence that was locally generated using a computerized algorithm. A blocked randomization approach with a block size of 2 was used to maintain balanced group sizes. The random allocation sequence was generated by a designated statistician who was not involved in patient enrollment or treatment administration. This study was conducted as a double-blind trial by protocol ensuring that participants, study personnel, and outcome assessors were blinded to the intervention allocation. No co-interventions were administered during the study. Population descriptives are presented as means with standard deviations (SD) for continuous variables and percentages for categorical variables. Treatment effects are reported with standard errors (SE) and 95% simultaneous confidence intervals (CI), as appropriate. Differences in outcomes between groups at discharge and follow-up were assessed using linear regression, with baseline values included as covariates to account for initial differences. An Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) was employed to compare group means while statistically controlling for baseline values. All analyses were done using a per-protocol approach. The statistical analysis followed a hierarchical approach to reduce multiple testing. The primary focus was to analyze the difference between the IG and the CG after completing the intervention (6 hand baths over 3 weeks). This analysis addressed the main hypothesis of the study and was the highest priority. If a significant difference was observed in the primary analysis (confirmatory), further analyses were conducted at the follow-up visits (4 weeks and 12 weeks post-intervention) (confirmatory). Should these analyses also show significant differences, exploratory analyses were performed to assess differences between groups after each individual intervention (hand baths 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5). No clustering by care providers or centers occurred in this study; thus, no adjustments for clustering were required. No subgroup analyses or additional adjusted analyses were conducted. Calculations were performed using R version 4.4.1 for Windows, alongside RTools 4.4 and RStudio (Version 2024.09.0+375; Released: 2024-09-23). Data availability statement The data associated with the paper are not publicly available but are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. Results Sixty-two patients were assessed for eligibility, fifty were enrolled, randomized and equally allocated to either the IG or the CG (sham). The IG received serial Bad Nauheim thermal brine hand baths (thermal). The CG received a sham intervention consisting of serial tap water hand baths (tap). Thirty-eight patients completed the whole trial and were analyzed. Only participants who completed the intervention and provided outcome data (N.=38) were included in the analysis, as no post-baseline data were available for early discontinuations (N.=12). The study was conducted over a 6-month period, from September to February 2023, amidst the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic ( ). Baseline patient and disease characteristics are shown in . Mean age was 72 years with most participants being female (N.=43, 86%). Mean disease duration (time since diagnosis) was 8 years with a symptom duration (mean) of 14 years ( ). The primary endpoint of the trial was met. After the intervention period the CG reported significantly higher VAS values (mean: 33.4, SE: 1.81, 95% CI: 29.8-37.1) compared to the IG (mean: 7.08, SE: 1.81, 95% CI: 3.4-10.8). The difference between groups was 26.4 points, which was statistically significant (SE: 1.81, 95% CI: 29.8-37.1; P<0.0001). The difference of 26.4 points on the VAS exceeds the minimum clinically important difference (MCID) of 20 mm. Auxiliary analysis showed significant differences between the IG and CG after the first hand bath. Pain reduction increased with each application, especially in the IG. At both follow-up visits (4 weeks and 12 weeks after intervention) the IG had significantly lower pain levels in comparison to the CG ( ). The AUSCAN pain subscore showed a significant reduction in pain (mean difference: 5.86, SE: 0.976, 95% CI: 3.88-7.84, P=<0.0001) in the IG (mean: 5.99, SE: 0.698, 95% CI: 4.57-7.41) vs. the CG (mean: 11.85, SE: 0.679, 95% CI: 10.47-13.23) after the interventions period, which supports the result of the primary outcome parameter. After 4 weeks and 12 weeks of follow-up and no intervention, there was no statistically significant difference between the two groups measured by AUSCAN. During the intervention period no significant differences in other AUSCAN subscales (function, stiffness, total score) were seen (Supplementary Digital Material

the CG ( ). The AUSCAN pain subscore showed a significant reduction in pain (mean difference: 5.86, SE: 0.976, 95% CI: 3.88-7.84, P=<0.0001) in the IG (mean: 5.99, SE: 0.698, 95% CI: 4.57-7.41) vs. the CG (mean: 11.85, SE: 0.679, 95% CI: 10.47-13.23) after the interventions period, which supports the result of the primary outcome parameter. After 4 weeks and 12 weeks of follow-up and no intervention, there was no statistically significant difference between the two groups measured by AUSCAN. During the intervention period no significant differences in other AUSCAN subscales (function, stiffness, total score) were seen (Supplementary Digital Material 1: Supplementary Table I). Regarding grip strength, measured using a hand dynamometer, both groups demonstrated a trend towards improvement for both hands. Statistically significant differences between groups were not observed, neither during the intervention period nor the follow-up (Supplementary Digital Material 2: Supplementary Table II). Parameters of microcirculation and tissue oxygenation (microvascular blood flow, postcapillary oxygen saturation [SO 2 ], and local hemoglobin content) or VEGF levels showed no statistically significant differences between groups during the intervention nor the follow-up period (Supplementary Digital Material 3: Supplementary Table III). The IG showed more favorable outcomes compared to the CG across all domains. In the general assessment, 13/18 (72%) of participants in the IG rated the intervention as “Very Good” or “Good,” compared to 10/19 (53%) in the CG, with one participant in the CG (5%) rating it as “Insufficient.” For pain relief, 13/18 (72%) in the IG rated it as “Very Good” or “Good,” while this was reported by only 6/19 (32%) in the CG (Supplementary Digital Material 4: Supplementary Table IV). No adverse events (AEs) or serious adverse events (SAEs) were reported by trial participants. The trial took place during the COVID-pandemic. There were 4 acute SARS-CoV2-infections in the IG and 5 in the CG. All infections were not deemed to be linked to the intervention. Discussion To the best of our knowledge, this is the first sham-controlled trial of thermal brine or thermal water hand baths in HOA. While balneotherapy is established in treating knee OA, , , - it’s role in treating HOA remains unclear. Patients treated with tbhb experienced a significant reduction in pain compared to patients treated with sham (tap water hand baths of the same temperature). Pain reduction was already significant and clinically relevant after the first intervention. Pain reduction was greater with every intervention and thus the primary endpoint (after 6 hand baths) was reached, showing pronounced statistical significance but also clinical relevance with a mean difference of 26 mm on VAS compared to sham. Follow-Up visits 4 weeks and 12 weeks after the intervention without any further physical or pharmacological treatment showed lasting effects with significantly lower pain levels in favour of the IG. Not only pain levels measured on VAS but also AUSCAN pain subscores were significantly lower after the intervention period in patients receiving tbhb. Thus tbhb seem to be a valuable treatment option in rehabilitation for HOA. Due to the rapid pain reduction tbhb seem a valid alternative to NSAID therapy with it’s possible life-threatening side effects. , When regarding subjective and individual perspectives, patients in the tbhb assessed interventions more favourable than patients receiving sham interventions. Tbhb was evaluated as effective and important. No AEs were reported, showing tbhb to be harmless. To investigate possible underlying mechanisms of the clinical effects of tbhb the study incorporated endpoints assessing parameters of microcirculation and tissue oxygenation (microvascular blood flow, postcapillary oxygen saturation and local hemoglobin content measured by O2C) and serum VEGF levels. The mechanisms underlying the pain-relieving effects of thermal brine and mineral water therapy are not yet fully understood. Mechanical, thermal and chemical factors play a role. Heat and water buoyancy help to reduce muscle tension and may increase the pain threshold of nociceptors. Likewise, changes at the molecular level in anti-inflammatory/inflammatory cytokines have recently become known that could explain the pain reduction. , Ingredients from thermal brine water can enter the systemic circulation via the skin, but the pathomechanisms are still largely unknown. Immersion during thermal mineral water therapy has many physiological effects and causes changes in the neuro-immuno-endocrine system. , When looking closely at the differences between tbhb and the chosen sham (covered tap water hand baths of the same temperature) mostly chemical differences appear. Bad Nauheimer thermal brine with its inherent temperature of 25 °C and the decision against artificial heating was used, which contains CO 2 . CO 2 can lead to vasodilation allowing better tissue microcirculation and possibly better oxygenation and ultimately less pain with VEGF playing an important role in this interplay. , However, O2C measurements did not show significant differences. In addition, VEGF serum levels were measured as VEGF is discussed as a modulator of pain in OA. , However, VEGF levels

tbhb and the chosen sham (covered tap water hand baths of the same temperature) mostly chemical differences appear. Bad Nauheimer thermal brine with its inherent temperature of 25 °C and the decision against artificial heating was used, which contains CO 2 . CO 2 can lead to vasodilation allowing better tissue microcirculation and possibly better oxygenation and ultimately less pain with VEGF playing an important role in this interplay. , However, O2C measurements did not show significant differences. In addition, VEGF serum levels were measured as VEGF is discussed as a modulator of pain in OA. , However, VEGF levels did not alter significantly between groups. Albeit, to exclude VEGF or microcirculation as underlying mechanisms of the profound clinical effects on pain of tbhb would be wrong. The time of day may have influenced the vascular response. Although all baths were administered in the morning hours from 9 to 12 a.m., it has been reported that skin perfusion after CO 2 baths peaks in early morning (around 7:00 a.m.) and declines toward noon, with only minor effects observed later in the day. In addition, the circulation-boosting effects of CO2 baths are temperature-dependent and do not occur at bath temperatures below 22 °C and are greatest at around 32-35 °C. Given the temperature of 25 °C of the used tbhb, the observed effect size may have been attenuated, potentially contributing to the null findings regarding O2C and VEGF, especially in light of the limited sample size. Stronger effects of CO 2 would be expected at higher temperatures or a larger sample size would be needed to observe significant effects on VEGF or O2C when using 25 °C thbh. Both VEGF and O2C were secondary (exploratory) outcomes, the study was primarily powered to detect a difference in pain (VAS). Non-pharmacological therapy trials impose a special challenge to trail design due to the nature of the physical intervention, which is challenging to blind correctly. , , In this trial special care was taken to plan and carry out a sham-controlled trial to ensure the validity of trial findings. , While tap water has been used as a sham for balneotherapy before, one needs to admit that it may induce more than a placebo. A sham intervention is a control procedure that mimics the physical aspects of the active treatment (such as temperature, immersion, or application method) but omits the presumed therapeutic component ( e.g. , mineral content, CO 2 or active mud ingredients). This may explain observed effects in the control group. However, when assessing effects and the between-group difference, verum and sham are clearly distinguishable. Thus, the choice of sham seems reasonable. The study was conducted during the COVID pandemic, which influenced recruitment negatively and may have introduced biases due to restricted access to care. Health regulations during the pandemic limited trial procedures, e.g. only one proband received an intervention at once. Still, acute SARS-CoV2 infection was the major reason for drop-out. In this regard, drop-out in general was more than expected. However, the actual effect size on pain (VAS) was higher than calculated. Therefore, the statistic was not compromised and significant differences could be measured with less probands to analyze. As interventions were carried out only on single probands, unblinding due to communication between probands during interventions was impossible. The study assesses short-term effects over a 3-week application (Supplementary Digital Material 5: Supplementary Figure 1). It remains unclear if effects expand further with prolonged application. However, even 6 applications of TBHH achieved a lasting relief in pain over 12 weeks. Although validated instruments were used to analyze pain, the perception of pain is a complex and highly subjective variable that can be influenced by several factors. In further studies the number and localization of the symptomatic joints should be assessed more closely. Furthermore, future trials should aim to include larger, more diverse cohorts and assess prolonged intervention schedules in a multicenter setting. The findings of this trial align with broader research on thermal mineral water therapy. Prior studies, particularly in knee OA, have shown comparable benefits for pain relief, function, and quality of life. , , , - , , When considering HOA in particular, two studies have applied somewhat comparable designs and methods . Kovács et al. showed that sulphurous thermal water hand baths (20 min/bath, 15 times over a period of 3 weeks) vs. warm tap water hand baths lead to less pain in the hand, more grip strength of both hands and better Health Assessment Questionnaire Disability Index (HAQ) and AUSCAN scores in patients with HOA. Horváth et al. showed, that patients treated with either thermal hand baths at 36 °C or 38 °C plus magnetotherapy improved the pinch strength of the right hand and HAQ better than magnetotherapy alone with significant effects over 13 weeks of follow-up.

Kovács et al. showed that sulphurous thermal water hand baths (20 min/bath, 15 times over a period of 3 weeks) vs. warm tap water hand baths lead to less pain in the hand, more grip strength of both hands and better Health Assessment Questionnaire Disability Index (HAQ) and AUSCAN scores in patients with HOA. Horváth et al. showed, that patients treated with either thermal hand baths at 36 °C or 38 °C plus magnetotherapy improved the pinch strength of the right hand and HAQ better than magnetotherapy alone with significant effects over 13 weeks of follow-up. In comparison to Horváth et al. our study used Bad Nauheimer thermal brine with an inherent temperature of 25 °C. We chose to not heat it artificially. Clinical effects are therefore possibly limited. Indeed, optimal temperatures for CO 2 baths are typically in the indifferent range (32-35 °C). According to Gutenbrunner et al. , microcirculatory responses at 22 °C reach only about one-tenth of those at 32 °C. In comparison however, we did not use any other intervention that could have influenced or even carried observed effects like Horváth et al. who added magnetotherapy. When comparing to Kovács et al. one must admit that different interventions were studied albeit both qualify as balneotherapy. In summary, this trial shows for the first time that in painful HOA serial thermal brine hand baths lead to a rapid pain relief with clinical benefit after the first intervention. After 6 interventions prolonged effects on pain can be observed over a 12 week follow-up. TBBH were without side effects and were rated with a convincing subjective satisfaction in the IG. Conclusions This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial demonstrates for the first time that serial thermal brine hand baths provide rapid, clinically relevant, and sustained pain relief in patients with hand osteoarthritis. Pain reduction was evident after the first application and increased with each subsequent intervention, with effects persisting for up to 12 weeks post-treatment. While no significant effects were observed on grip strength, microcirculation, or VEGF levels, the intervention was safe, well-tolerated, and rated favorably by participants. The lack of changes in mechanistic endpoints may be attributed to the moderate bath temperature and limited sample size. Given its simplicity, absence of adverse events, and high patient acceptance, thermal brine therapy represents a promising non-pharmacological adjunct for managing hand osteoarthritis. Future studies should confirm these findings in larger cohorts, explore optimal temperature settings, and further elucidate the underlying mechanisms of action. chunks.content: Introduction Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem autoimmune disease that predominantly affects the younger population. Despite the emergence of novel therapeutics in recent decades, the survival of SLE fails to improve further since the mid-1990s. Mortality in SLE is attributed to disease or treatment related complications. Among patients with common rheumatic musculoskeletal diseases (RMDs), SLE has the highest standardized mortality ratio compared to the general population, with infection being the leading cause of death. In more recent cohort studies which showed improved survival of SLE compared with historical cohorts, infection still accounted for more than half of the deaths. The heightened susceptibility to infective complications in SLE patients is multi-factorial. A myriad of immune aberrations, especially during disease activity, are reported in SLE. These include reduced number and dysfunction of the immune cells such as the lymphocytes, neutrophils, macrophages and natural killer (NK) cells, as well as hypogammaglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, impaired complement function and functional asplenia. The use of systemic glucocorticoids (GCs), non-GC immunosuppressive agents, and the biologic/targeted drugs, along with other disease or treatment related comorbidities such as chronic kidney disease and diabetes mellitus, further aggravate the infection risk. SLE patients are prone to a broad spectrum of common and opportunistic micro-organisms. About two-third of infections in SLE were caused by bacteria affecting the respiratory and urinary tracts, 27% were caused by fungal organisms involving the respiratory tract, and 10% were caused by viral infection of the respiratory tract and skin. Opportunistic infections that were frequently reported in SLE include Legionella pneumophila, Listeria monocytogenes, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, cytomegalovirus, herpes zoster and invasive fungal organisms, such as Candida, Cryptococcus, and Aspergillus species, which are associated with high mortality. , A meta-analysis revealed a pooled risk ratios of 3.0 for severe infections overall, 6.1 for tuberculosis, 2.6 for pneumonia and 2.5 for herpes zoster (HZ) in SLE patients compared with the general population. Kidney involvement, high disease activity, renal insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, organ damage, lymphopenia and immunosuppressive therapies were major risk factors for severe infections in SLE. , Preventing infective complications in SLE is the key to improve the survival of the disease. This can be achieved by several means: (1) judicious use of GCs and immunosuppressive agents; (2) prophylaxis against micro-organisms and early recognition of infection; and (3) vaccination. As periods of heavy immunosuppression are inevitable for the initial treatment of various serious manifestations of SLE, and the long-term use of anti-microbial prophylaxis is limited by tolerability and microbial resistance, vaccination remains the most important strategy for reducing infection risk in SLE patients. Despite the clear benefit of vaccines, hesitancy to vaccination is prevalent in patients with SLE according to multiple cross-sectional surveys. This phenomenon reflects the concern regarding efficacy and safety of vaccines, including the potential risk of disease flares. In particular, the B-cell depleting agents are well recognized to greatly reduce the humoral responses to the COVID-19 and pneumococcal vaccines, leading to futility of vaccination in a substantial proportion of patients. Overall, reluctance from patients, resistance from physicians in recommending vaccination, cost of vaccines and relative contraindication to the live vaccines are obstacles to vaccination in SLE. This article summarizes the current evidence of efficacy and safety of common vaccines in SLE, and recommendations for their use from major guidelines ( ). Efficacy and safety of common vaccines in SLE SARS-CoV2 vaccine The global COVID-19 epidemic was caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV2). A meta-analysis in the year 2021 reported a pooled point prevalence of 0.011 of COVID-19 infection among patients with RMDs, with higher rates observed in the subgroups of SLE, Sjogren’s disease and systemic sclerosis (0.034). The risk of having COVID-19 infection was at least one-fold higher in these patients than the control population (OR 2.19[1.05–4.58]). Patients with RMDs infected with SARS-CoV2 had higher rates of hospitalization and mortality, which was associated with the use of GCs, conventional synthetic disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) with or without the biologic/targeted DMARDs. Immunogenicity and safety of SARS-CoV2 vaccine Dozens of COVID-19 vaccines have been approved up to 2025, including the mRNA, protein subunit, viral-vector and inactivated whole-virus vaccines. Currently, the mRNA and protein-based vaccines dominate due to their strong immunogenicity and adaptability to emergent strains. The vaccine formulation evolves yearly to match the prevalent SARS-CoV2 variants, from Delta and Omicron to XBB.1.5 and now JN.1-lineage derivatives. In addition to being an exogenous neoantigen, mRNA vaccines are hypothesized to trigger flares of autoimmune diseases by inducing oxidation-mediated DNA damage, which promotes interferon (IFN) gene expression and leads to autoantibody production. Moreover, the encoding of the SARS-CoV2 spike (S) protein and the adjuvant activity from these vaccines activates the toll-like receptors (TLRs) on dendritic cells, causing expansion of the S-protein-specific effector and follicular T cells that further augment the activity of the autoreactive B cells. ,

In addition to being an exogenous neoantigen, mRNA vaccines are hypothesized to trigger flares of autoimmune diseases by inducing oxidation-mediated DNA damage, which promotes interferon (IFN) gene expression and leads to autoantibody production. Moreover, the encoding of the SARS-CoV2 spike (S) protein and the adjuvant activity from these vaccines activates the toll-like receptors (TLRs) on dendritic cells, causing expansion of the S-protein-specific effector and follicular T cells that further augment the activity of the autoreactive B cells. , Flares of the underlying RMDs after mRNA SARS-CoV2 vaccination were reported to occur in 0–69% of patients, but most flares did not warrant a change in treatment. In patients with SLE, a systematic review revealed disease flares in 5.5% of patients at 14–90 d after SARS-CoV2 vaccination. Similarly, the majority of flares was mild/moderate and serious life-threatening flares were exceedingly infrequent (0–2%). Anti-dsDNA positivity, high disease activity and the use of AZA or belimumab pre-vaccination were risk factors for SLE flares after SARS-CoV2 vaccination. Cases of new-onset SLE after SARS-CoV2 vaccination have been reported, mostly after the first dose of BioNTech vaccine. Moreover, a nationwide study in Korea reported an increased incidence of SLE in the subsequent year following mRNA SARS-CoV2 vaccination compared to non-vaccinated historical cohort (HR 1.16[1.02–1.32]). On the other hand, several cases of de novo SLE or lupus nephritis shortly after SARS-CoV-2 infection in previously healthy individuals have been reported in the literature, suggesting the viral infection itself may trigger systemic autoimmunity. , A systematic review of population-based cohort studies showed an increased risk of SLE after SARS-CoV2 infection in a pooled analysis (RR 3.17[2.25–4.48]). In a retrospective study involving 273 SLE patients, those experienced with SARS-CoV-2 infection had a significantly higher incidence of clinical flares within 90 d compared with matched non-infected controls (17.6% versus 5.5%; OR 3.67[1.59–8.46]). This illustrates that reducing the occurrence of SARS-CoV2 infection by vaccination outweighs the potential risk of vaccine-induced disease flares. Most patients with SLE are able to mount an adequate immune response to the COVID-19 vaccines. The pooled seropositivity rate after full vaccination in 17 studies was 81.1%, with higher rate after mRNA than the inactivated viral and viral vector vaccines. The breakthrough COVID-19 infection rates were generally low after vaccination, ranging from 0 to 6% in these studies. On the other hand, rituximab (RTX) has been shown to significantly impair the humoral response to COVID-19 vaccination in patients with RMDs including SLE, with a low seropositivity rate of 39% with RTX monotherapy and 36% when combined with methotrexate (MTX). Belimumab, a monoclonal antibody against BAFF, is increasing used in patients with SLE, including lupus nephritis. A recent study showed that the positive antibody response to COVID-19 vaccines (92% mRNA-based vaccines, 8% vector-based vaccine) in belimumab (87%) and non-belimumab (85%) treated SLE patients were similar. Among 30 patients in the belimumab group, only two failed to produce antibodies against SARS-CoV2 after three doses of the vaccines. Notably, these patients had been previously treated with RTX. Tixagevimab–cilgavimab, a monoclonal antibody combination for COVID-19 pre-exposure prophylaxis, may be considered as an alternative in patients who do not mount an adequate humoral response or who are contraindicated to the COVID-19 vaccines. A recent study of 330 rheumatic patients receiving RTX, one dose of tixagevimab–cilgavimab was well tolerated and effective in reducing new COVID-19 infection in the subsequent 3 months. Recommendation of COVID-19 vaccination in SLE The European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) recommends patients with RMDs to receive any locally approved SARS-CoV2 vaccines, ideally during a quiescent phase and before commencement or augmentation of immunosuppression. In patients receiving anti-CD20 therapies, SARS-CoV2 vaccination should be scheduled in a way to optimize vaccine immunogenicity. Despite limited evidence, a third primary dose of SARS-CoV2 vaccine may be considered according to national guidelines in patients receiving certain immunosuppressive agents such as higher doses of GCs, anti‑CD20 biologics and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) who are expected to have more rapid waning of the vaccine response. The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) provides a more detailed recommendation on the schedule of existing immunosuppressive therapies and timing of COVID-19 vaccination. Certain immunosuppressants may be withheld 1–2 weeks post-vaccination if disease activity allows, including most conventional immunosuppressive (e.g. MMF, MTX, azathioprine, calcineurin inhibitors) and biologic/targeted agents (e.g. abatacept, belimumab, Janus kinase [JAK] inhibitors) despite the evidence is mixed. If feasible, intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses should be timed to occur approximately 1 week after each vaccine dose. For RTX users, vaccination should ideally be scheduled 2–4 weeks before the next anticipated dose of the biologic. For patients under heavy immunosuppression, additional booster vaccine doses should be considered. If feasible, intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses should be timed to occur approximately 1 week after each vaccine dose. For RTX users, vaccination should ideally be scheduled 2–4 weeks before the next anticipated dose of the biologic. For patients under heavy immunosuppression, additional booster vaccine doses should be considered. Influenza vaccine Seasonal influenza vaccines are formulated annually to protect against the most prevalent circulating strains. While monovalent or bivalent vaccines were developed for pandemic situations, current seasonal influenza vaccine formulations are trivalent or quadrivalent, targeting two influenza A and one or two influenza B serotypes, respectively. Three kinds of influenza vaccines are available: (1) inactivated vaccine; (2) recombinant vaccine; and (3) live-attenuated vaccine. In addition, high-dose (4 times antigen than standard dose) and adjuvanted formulation of inactivated influenza vaccines have been developed to enhance immunogenicity. Despite the long history of the influenza vaccines, the vaccination rate remains low among patients with SLE. In a survey conducted in mainland China, the uptake of influenza vaccine in SLE patients was only 8.3%. Similarly, a recent cross-sectional survey from Saudi Arabia reported only 27.6% of SLE and RA patients had received influenza vaccination in the preceding two seasons. Notably, only 51% of the respondents believed that the influenza vaccine is safe and effective. Immunogenicity and safety of the influenza vaccine The immunogenicity of the standard-dose influenza vaccine is lower in SLE patients than healthy individuals. In two meta-analysis studies, , SLE patients were shown to have significantly lower sero-protection rates (defined as serum antibody titer of no less than 1:40 after vaccination) to H1N1 and H3N2 virus; and sero-conversion rates (defined as greater than 4-fold increase in antibody titer) to H1N1 and influenza B viral serotypes. Additional booster dose of the vaccine did not improve immunogenicity in SLE patients except in those who did not have vaccination in the preceding year. Despite reduced immunogenicity, pooling of the data from 45 studies involving 16,596 SLE patients showed that breakthrough influenza infection rate remained significantly reduced in vaccinated than non-vaccinated SLE patients. In addition, disease activity score of SLE did not change significantly post-vaccination, and flares of SLE, if occurred, were generally mild to moderate. Recommendation of influenza vaccination in SLE The EULAR recommends influenza vaccination in the majority of patients with RMDs during disease quiescence. The ACR recommends to use the high-dose or adjuvanted influenza vaccines in patients with RMDs unless they are unavailable. Although no studies of high-dose influenza vaccines have been published in SLE patients, these vaccines are shown to achieve higher immunogenicity than standard-dose vaccines in rheumatoid arthritis patients and other immunocompromised groups such as solid organ transplant recipients. Pneumococcal vaccine Respiratory tract infection is a major cause of severe infections in patients with SLE. In a multi-center Spanish study, the most frequent infective complication experienced by 3,658 SLE patients after a mean follow-up of 10 y was respiratory tract infections (35.5%), followed by urinary tract (15.0%) and soft tissue infections (13.3%). Bacteria accounted for 52% and viruses accounted for 12% of the infective episodes. Among bacterial pathogens, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest organism causing lower respiratory tract infection. This underscores the importance of pneumococcal vaccination in patients with SLE. There are two types of pneumococcal vaccines: pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV) and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV). PPSV is composed of pneumococcal capsular polysaccharides and PPSV23 is the only available formulation containing 23 serotypes of pneumococcal polysaccharides. PCV consists of pneumococcal capsular polysaccharides conjugated to a protein. The original PCV7, which consists of seven serotypes of pneumococcal capsules, was replaced by PCV13. Meanwhile, PCV10 is mainly used in childhood vaccination programs in some countries. More recently, there are higher-valent conjugate vaccine containing 15 (PCV15), 20 (PCV20) and 21 (PCV21) serotypes. The conventional PPSV leads to a B cell response characterized by a predominant IgM and short-lived IgG antibody production with low frequency of memory B cell generation, which explains their limited durability of immunogenicity after 3–5 y. In contrast, chemical conjugation of pneumococcal polysaccharide to a carrier protein in PCV induces a T-cell-dependent immune response, leading to an increased serotype-specific memory B cell response and a booster effect upon subsequent antigen exposure. Traditionally, a prime‑boost strategy (PCV followed by PPSV23) is recommended to broaden the serotype coverage. With the introduction of higher-valent PCVs, a single-dose approach may be sufficient for most adults. , Thus, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) suggests a single dose of PCV20 or PCV21 for individuals aged ≥65 y. Traditionally, a prime‑boost strategy (PCV followed by PPSV23) is recommended to broaden the serotype coverage. With the introduction of higher-valent PCVs, a single-dose approach may be sufficient for most adults. , Thus, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) suggests a single dose of PCV20 or PCV21 for individuals aged ≥65 y. Despite the high prevalence of pneumococcal infection in SLE, the vaccination rate remains low. According to a survey conducted in China, the pneumococcal vaccine uptake was only 1.7%, with the top reasons for vaccine hesitancy being concerns about SLE flares and other adverse effects, and the lack of awareness regarding vaccine availability. Another survey conducted in Japan reported that the most common reason for reluctance to pneumococcal vaccination in SLE patients was the lack of full reimbursement from the national health insurance scheme and other public fundings. Immunogenicity and safety of the pneumococcal vaccine A meta-analysis has identified 18 studies on immunogenicity and safety of the pneumococcal vaccines in SLE. Overall, no serious adverse events were reported, and around one-third of patients suffered from minor complaints. The vaccine immunogenicity in terms of the achievement of protective antibody titers varied from 36% to 98%. Factors associated with reduced vaccine efficacy included high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), older age, earlier SLE onset, high disease activity, and use of immunosuppressive therapy at the time of vaccination. Among the included studies, Nagel et al. observed that SLE patients receiving belimumab in addition to the standard of care maintained adequate post-vaccination antibody titers compared to healthy individuals. This observation is further supported by an open randomized study, which showed preserved vaccine responses to belimumab regardless of the timing of vaccination (4 weeks prior to or 24 weeks after belimumab administration). The primed-boost vaccination strategy of pneumococcal vaccination has been evaluated in SLE patients. In the multicenter, double-blind randomized controlled trial (VACCILUP) in patients with SLE, no significant enhancement in immunogenicity was observed when PCV7 was administered prior to PPSV23 (PCV7/PPSV23) compared to PPSV23 alone. Consistent findings were reported in a non-randomized comparative study of these two strategies. Compared to PPSV23 alone, administration of PCV10 preceding PPSV23 (PCV10/PPSV23) did not yield significantly higher serotype-specific IgG anti-pneumococcal antibodies. Finally, a single-center study in Brazil reported a more robust vaccine response with the PCV13-priming and PPSV23-boost strategy than the two vaccines administered in a reversed sequence (PPSV23 followed by PCV13). Recommendation of pneumococcal vaccination in SLE Both EULAR and ACR strongly recommend patients on immunosuppressants to receive pneumococcal vaccine during disease quiescence. The EULAR recommends PCV13 prime-PPSV23 boost strategy with an interval of at least 8 weeks between the vaccinations, whereas the ACR suggests to follow the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guideline when choosing a specific pneumococcal vaccination strategy as there are emerging types of PCVs. Whereas the prime-boost pneumococcal vaccination strategy has not demonstrated clear benefit in terms of vaccine immunogenicity in SLE patients, further studies on the efficacy of the higher-valent conjugate vaccines such as PCV20 and PCV21 as single-dose regimens are warranted. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes a respiratory tract infection that affects all age groups. It accounts for at least 470,000 hospitalizations and 33,000 in-hospital deaths of older adults (≥60 y) per annum in high-income countries. While classically associated with bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants, RSV is increasingly recognized as a major disease burden in older adults, and patients with chronic cardiopulmonary conditions and immunocompromised states. In susceptible patients, RSV may cause a severe lower respiratory tract infection, precipitate secondary bacterial infections and lead to respiratory failure. In a study of 188 patients with RMDs, the 90-d mortality was 6% among all patients and 12.5% among those hospitalized. Older age, frailty, greater comorbidity burden and concurrent infection were associated with increased risk of hospitalization after RSV infection. Immunogenicity and safety of the RSV vaccine There are currently three United States (US) Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved RSV vaccines (Abrysvo, Arexvy and mResvia) for adults aged ≥60 y. Abrysvo is a bivalent subunit vaccine containing the pre-fusion (pre-F) forms of RSV-A and RSV-B F glycoproteins. It is also approved for pregnant women to confer passive neonatal protection. Arexvy is a subunit vaccine containing a stabilized trimeric pre-F protein (RSVPreF3) combined with the AS01E adjuvant system, which enhances both humoral and cellular immune responses. mResvia is a messenger RNA vaccine encoding the membrane-anchored pre-F protein derived from RSV-A. Pivotal phase 3 trials have demonstrated high efficacy and safety of the RSV vaccines in adults aged ≥60 y. Abrysvo showed a vaccine efficacy of 85.7% against RSV-associated lower respiratory tract illness and 62.1% against RSV-associated acute respiratory illness. On the

On the other hand, a single dose of Arexvy provided a vaccine efficacy of 82.6% against RT-PCR-confirmed RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease and 94.1% against severe RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease in adults. In a subsequent RCT, the vaccine was also demonstrated to provide sustained protection against RSV infection over three seasons. Finally, mResvia, demonstrated a vaccine efficacy of 83.7% and 82.4%, respectively, against RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease with at least two and three signs or symptoms in adults aged ≥60 y. The phase 3 MONeT study evaluated the efficacy and safety of a single dose of Abrysvo in adults 18–59 y of age with chronic or immunocompromised health conditions, including chronic pulmonary, cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, neurologic, hematologic and metabolic disorders (e.g. diabetes mellitus). Results demonstrated non-inferiority of vaccine immunogenicity in these patients compared to that observed in adults aged ≥60 y, supporting the use of RSV vaccine in younger high-risk populations. Another phase 3 single-arm study demonstrated good immune responses of Abrysvo in immunocompromised and renally impaired adults with no safety concerns. The indication of Arexvy has recently been expanded to adults 18–49 y of age who are at risk of RSV disease. This is supported by a phase 3 trial which demonstrated non-inferior immune response of the vaccine in these patients compared to adults aged ≥60 y. The at-risk population included chronic pulmonary and cardiovascular illnesses, diabetes mellitus, chronic liver and kidney diseases, and active/chronic neurological/neuromuscular conditions. Recommendation of RSV vaccination The US CDC recommends a single dose of RSV vaccine for all adults aged ≥75 y and 50–74 y at risk of severe RSV illness. Moreover, RSV vaccination is recommended by over 20 countries for older adults and adults at risk. These recommendations differ across countries, with varying age threshold and risk-based indications for RSV vaccination. In pregnant women, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends administration of RSV vaccine in the third trimester to protect infants from infection through transplacental antibodies. There are still no major RSV vaccine trials in patients with SLE. However, given their immunocompromised status, SLE patients, particularly those treated with the type I IFN antagonists that weaken viral defense, should consider RSV vaccination. Herpes zoster (HZ) vaccine HZ results from reactivation of the latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection (chickenpox). HZ reactivation is more common in older individuals and immunocompromised subgroups, such as those receiving chemotherapy, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, diabetes mellitus, and cancer. HZ infection may cause extensive (≥3 dermatomes) local disease, systemic dissemination and mortality in immunocompromised patients. The prevalence of HZ infection is high in patients with SLE. Up to 47% of SLE patients developed HZ infection during their course of illness and the reported incidence rate ranged from 6.4 to 91.4 per 1,000 patient-years. A longitudinal study involving 1,485 SLE patients, with an average disease duration of 13.9 y, reported an age-adjusted HZ incidence of 12.0 per 1,000 person-years, which was significantly higher than that of age-matched controls with non-inflammatory musculoskeletal diseases (8.7 per 1,000 person-years; HR 1.7[1.1–2.7]). Among patients with chronic medical illnesses, the pooled relative risk of HZ was greatest in those with SLE (RR 2.1[1.4–3.2]), followed by RA (RR 1.7[1.4–2.0]), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (RR 1.3[1.2–1.4]), diabetes mellitus (RR 1.3[1.2–1.5]), and asthma (RR 1.3[1.1–1.4]). Risk factors for HZ reactivation in SLE patients include renal involvement, lymphopenia and the use of immunosuppressive agents such as GCs, cyclophosphamide, MMF, azathioprine and anifrolumab. Anifrolumab is a type I interferon receptor antagonist approved for the treatment of moderate-to-severe active non-renal SLE. Across the pivotal phase II and III trials of anifrolumab in SLE (MUSE, TULIP-1, and TULIP-2), the annualized incidence of HZ was 6.1%, which was higher than those assigned to the placebo (PBO) group (1.3%). Most HZ events were mild or moderate and resolved without treatment discontinuation. Despite the high rate of HZ infection in SLE, vaccination rates were reported to be as low as 7.1%. HZ has been linked to lupus flares, which may contribute to vaccine hesitancy in SLE patients. Other barriers to HZ vaccination include lack of awareness, perceived safety risks of the live HZ vaccine, and the lack of reimbursement by the health care system. Despite the high rate of HZ infection in SLE, vaccination rates were reported to be as low as 7.1%. HZ has been linked to lupus flares, which may contribute to vaccine hesitancy in SLE patients. Immunogenicity and safety of the HZ vaccines Currently, there are two types of HZ vaccines: a live attenuated VZV vaccine (Zostavax) and a subunit recombinant vaccine containing VZV glycoprotein E and the AS01B adjuvant system (Shingrix). The live HZ vaccine is generally not recommended in immunocompromised hosts as it may introduce infection. A pilot study of 10 SLE patients vaccinated with Zostavax reported no incident cases of HZ, disseminated infection, or lupus flare within 12 weeks of vaccination. Although vaccine immunogenicity was reduced in SLE patients compared with controls, a similar proportion of SLE and controls demonstrated a >50% increase in cellular immunity after vaccination. In an RCT of Zostavax in 90 SLE patients, no increase in disease flare was demonstrated in vaccinated than PBO-treated patients. At 6 weeks post-vaccination, humoral immunity (anti-VZV IgG reactivity) increased by 60% and cell-mediated immunity (VZV-stimulated IFN-γ enzyme-linked ELISPOT assay) increased by 42% in the vaccine group, compared to minimal changes in the PBO group. A 5-y extension of the same study demonstrated preserved immunogenicity of Zostavax in SLE patients. The anti-VZV IgG levels and T-cell responses remained significantly higher in vaccinated SLE than placebo-treated SLE patients, indicating durable vaccine immunogenicity. One vaccinated patient (3.1%) and three PBO-treated patients (7.9%) experienced HZ reactivation, but the difference was not statistically significant. The recombinant subunit HZ vaccine has proven efficacy in two pivotal RCTs , in reducing HZ infection by 97.2% among individuals ≥50 y and 91.3% in those ≥70 y of age. The efficacy of Shingrix in SLE was demonstrated by a recent RCT from South Korea. A total of 65 patients with stable SLE received 2 doses of either vaccine or PBO 8 weeks apart. A positive humoral response (≥4-fold increase in anti-glycoprotein E antibody) was achieved in 98% of vaccinated patients compared to 0% in the PBO group ( p < .0001) 4 weeks after the second dose. Moreover, cell-mediated response (glycoprotein E-specific T-cell responses) was significantly higher in vaccinated than PBO-treated patients (67% vs 18%; p = .01). No significant increase in SLE activity or flares were observed in vaccinated SLE patients over 1 y. The HZ was generally well-tolerated. A more recent multi-center PBO-controlled RCT conducted in South America demonstrated immunogenicity and safety of the recombinant subunit HZ vaccine in patients with RMDs within 6 weeks after completion of vaccination. Among 1,136 patients recruited in this study, 336 (29.6%) had underlying SLE. Although the study was not powered to evaluate disease subgroups, it confirms short-term safety of the HZ vaccine in patients with RMDs in terms of not leading to worsening of disease activity. Recommendations of HZ vaccination in SLE The EULAR recommends that HZ vaccination in high-risk RMD patients, including SLE. The recombinant zoster vaccine is preferred to the live-attenuated vaccine. The ACR recommends the recombinant HZ vaccine in adults ≥18 y with RMDs who are receiving immunosuppressive therapy. Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine Cervical cancer is strongly linked to persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). High-risk HPV serotypes express viral oncoprotein and drive the development of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia than may progress invasive carcinoma. In contrast, low-risk HPV serotypes are typically found in benign lesions such as genital warts. Out of the more than 200 known HPV genotypes, types 16 and 18 have the strongest oncogenic potential, while 10 other genotypes are also classified carcinogenic. A meta-analysis reported a pooled cervical HPV prevalence of 15.3% (0.79–27.8%) in healthy women versus 34.2% (19.6–52.5%) in patients with SLE. Overall, women with SLE had 1.87-times significantly higher risk of having cervical HPV infection. As a result, women with SLE have a significantly elevated risk of cervical cancer compared to the general population (RR 1.7[1.2–2.4]). These findings support the importance of HPV vaccination and regular cervical screening in SLE patients. Immunogenicity and safety of the vaccine There are three HPV vaccines available in the market: bivalent (2vHPV), quadrivalent (4vHPV), and nonavalent (9vHPV). Concerns regarding their safety in SLE have been raised, largely based on theoretical risks of molecular mimicry between HPV vaccine antigens and host proteins, which may trigger SLE onset in susceptible individuals. , However, subsequent large studies did not show an increased risk of SLE development after HPV vaccination.
